title: Feedback loops: how bodies and machines sense, decide and correct

summary.text: You can balance a long stick on your palm for many seconds, but a pencil falls almost at once. Why is the short one harder? In this lesson you will test sticks of three lengths, measure what your pulse does when you stand up, and find the same three-part loop in your body, in an electric iron and in a flush tank.
summary.art: A girl balancing a metre-long stick upright on her open palm while watching its top, with a pencil lying fallen on the floor beside her and an electric iron and a flush tank drawn small in the background.

intro.hook: Stand a pencil upright on your open palm and let go with the other hand. Try to keep the pencil standing. How long did it stay up? Now guess: would a stick as long as your arm be easier or harder? Say why you think so.
intro.text: Most people guess that the long stick is harder, because it is bigger and heavier. You will test that guess in the Stick Test. To keep anything steady, three jobs must be done again and again. Something must notice a change. Something must decide what to do. Something must act. Your body does these three jobs for your warmth, your blood pressure and your blood sugar. An iron, a fridge and a flush tank do them too. In this lesson you find the three jobs in each one, and you find out what happens when one job is missing or late.
intro.art: A child's open palm with a pencil standing on it, leaning a little, and the child's eyes wide with concentration.

outcomes: By the end I can name the three jobs in a feedback loop, which are sensor, control centre and effector, and say what each one does.
By the end I can tell a closed loop from an open loop by asking whether news of the result comes back.
By the end I can explain, from my Stick Test, why a loop fails when its news is missing or arrives too late.
By the end I can trace the loop that keeps blood reaching my brain when I stand up.
By the end I can find the sensor, the control and the effector in an iron, a fridge and a flush tank.
By the end I can compare on-off control with how-much control, and say what each one is good for.
By the end I can give examples of feedback loops at many sizes: one cell, one body, one machine and perhaps the whole Earth.
By the end I can plan a fair test, repeat it, find a mean, and write my claim, evidence and reasoning.

terms.meaning: Homeostasis is the way a living body keeps its inside conditions within safe limits while the outside keeps changing. The word was made from Greek words meaning 'similar' and 'staying'.
terms.example: Your body stays close to 37 degrees Celsius in a cold cinema hall and on a hot May afternoon in Chennai.
terms.art: A child in a sweater in a cold room and the same child in a hot street, with the same small '37' written on the chest in both.

terms.meaning: Feedback is news about the result of an action that comes back and changes the next action.
terms.example: When you pour tea, you watch the level rise. That sight is feedback, and it tells your hand when to stop.
terms.art: A hand pouring tea into a glass tumbler, with a curved arrow from the tea level back to the child's eye.

terms.meaning: A feedback loop is a circle of cause and effect. A change is sensed, a response is made, the response alters the change, and the altered change is sensed again.
terms.example: Fridge warms, thermostat senses it, motor runs, fridge cools, thermostat senses that, motor stops.
terms.art: Four arrows in a circle joining the words change, sensor, control and effector.

terms.meaning: Negative feedback is feedback that acts against a change, so the level comes back towards where it was. 'Negative' here means 'opposite', not 'bad'.
terms.example: You get hot, so you sweat, and the sweating cools you.
terms.art: An arrow pushing a level up and a second arrow from a loop pushing it back down.

terms.meaning: A sensor is a part that detects one kind of change and reports it. In the body, a sensor is also called a receptor.
terms.example: Warmth sensors in your skin report to your brain when your skin heats up.
terms.art: A close-up of skin with a small nerve ending under it, and a wavy heat line above.

terms.meaning: A control centre is the part that receives the report, compares it with the level that is needed, and sends out an order.
terms.example: The brainstem compares your blood pressure with what is needed and orders your heart to speed up.
terms.art: A brain seen from the side with the brainstem at its base coloured, and arrows going in and out.

terms.meaning: An effector is a part that carries out the order and so changes the level. Muscles and glands are the body's effectors.
terms.example: Sweat glands are effectors. So is the heart muscle.
terms.art: A sweat gland drawn as a coiled tube opening on the skin, with a drop of sweat at the top.

terms.meaning: A response is what the effector does.
terms.example: Shivering is a response to cold. A faster pulse is a response to standing up.
terms.art: A child shivering with small movement lines round the shoulders.

terms.meaning: A set point is the level that a loop works to keep. In a machine it is set by a dial. In the body it is a useful idea, and scientists still argue about what makes it.
terms.example: An iron's dial at 'cotton' sets a higher set point than the dial at 'nylon'.
terms.art: The dial of an electric iron with fabric names round it and a finger turning it.

terms.meaning: In a loop, the error is the gap between the level now and the set point. It does not mean a mistake.
terms.example: The room is at 29 degrees and the AC is set to 24 degrees. The error is 5 degrees.
terms.art: Two marks on a thermometer, one labelled 'now' and one labelled 'wanted', with a bracket between them.

terms.meaning: A disturbance is anything from outside the loop that pushes the level away from the set point.
terms.example: Opening the fridge door lets warm air in. That is a disturbance for the fridge.
terms.art: An open fridge door with warm air drawn as wavy arrows going in.

terms.meaning: A closed loop is a system in which news of the result comes back and changes the action.
terms.example: A geyser with a thermostat stops heating when the water is hot enough.
terms.art: A water heater with an arrow from the hot water back to a small switch.

terms.meaning: An open loop is a system that acts without checking its own result.
terms.example: A mixer-grinder runs for as long as you hold the switch, whether the chutney is smooth or not.
terms.art: A mixer-grinder with a single straight arrow from switch to jar and no arrow coming back.

terms.meaning: Delay is the time a loop takes to go once round, from sensing a change to finishing the response.
terms.example: It takes you about a fifth of a second to see a stick lean and start to move your hand.
terms.art: A stopwatch beside a leaning stick and a hand that has only just begun to move.

terms.meaning: On-off control is control with only two responses, fully on and fully off.
terms.example: An iron's heater is either on or off. The iron's temperature goes up and down a little round the set point.
terms.art: A zigzag line wobbling above and below a straight dotted line.

terms.meaning: How-much control makes the response bigger when the error is bigger and smaller when the error is smaller. Engineers call it proportional control.
terms.example: You sweat a little on a warm day and a lot after running in the sun.
terms.art: A small drop beside a small sun and many drops beside a large sun.

terms.meaning: A baroreceptor is a sensor in the wall of a large artery that reports how much the blood is stretching the wall. An artery is a tube that carries blood away from the heart.
terms.example: Baroreceptors in the arteries of your neck report a drop in pressure when you stand up.
terms.art: The side of a neck with an artery inside it and a small patch on the artery wall marked with nerve endings.

terms.meaning: The brainstem is the lowest part of the brain, where it joins the spinal cord. It holds the control centres for heartbeat, blood pressure and breathing.
terms.example: Your brainstem adjusts your heart while you sleep.
terms.art: A brain seen from the side with the stalk at its base coloured and labelled.

terms.meaning: The hypothalamus is a part of the brain about the size of an almond, deep in the middle. It holds control centres for warmth, thirst and hunger.
terms.example: When your blood becomes a little too salty, the hypothalamus makes you feel thirsty.
terms.art: A brain cut down the middle with a small almond-sized part near the centre coloured.

terms.meaning: A thermostat is a device that senses temperature and switches a heater or cooler on and off to keep the temperature near a set point.
terms.example: The thermostat in a fridge starts the motor when the inside warms up.
terms.art: The inside wall of a fridge with a small numbered dial.

terms.meaning: A bimetallic strip is two different metals joined along their length. One metal grows more than the other when heated, so the strip bends.
terms.example: Inside an iron, a bimetallic strip bends as it heats and pulls a switch open.
terms.art: A straight two-coloured metal strip, and the same strip bent into a curve above a small flame.

terms.meaning: A float valve is a tap opened and closed by a float that rides on the water.
terms.example: In a flush tank, the float rises with the water and shuts the tap when the tank is full.
terms.art: The inside of a flush tank with a ball float on an arm joined to an inlet tap.

terms.meaning: A governor is a device that keeps the speed of an engine steady.
terms.example: On James Watt's steam engines, two spinning metal balls swung outwards as the engine sped up, and that closed the steam valve a little.
terms.art: Two metal balls on hinged arms spinning round an upright rod on top of an old steam engine.

terms.meaning: Cybernetics is the study of control and feedback in animals, including humans, and in machines. Norbert Wiener named it in 1948 from the Greek word for a person who steers a boat.
terms.example: A cybernetics question: what do a thermostat and the hypothalamus have in common?
terms.art: A woman steering a small boat with an oar at the back, looking at a far tree.

explanations.concept: Every feedback loop has three jobs
explanations.definition: A feedback loop needs a sensor to detect a change, a control centre to compare and decide, and an effector to act. The result of the action is then sensed again.
explanations.description: Think of pouring water to a line. Your eyes detect the level. Your brain compares the level with the line and decides. Your hand tips the jug or stops. Then your eyes look again. These are the three jobs, and they repeat in a circle. Homeostasis works the same way. For your warmth, the sensors are nerve endings in the skin and in the brain that respond to temperature. The control centre is in the hypothalamus. The effectors are sweat glands, the muscles round the small blood vessels of your skin, and the big muscles that shiver. Why three jobs and not two? Without a sensor, nothing knows there is a change. Without a comparison, nothing knows which way to act, or when to stop. Without an effector, nothing changes. Take away any one, and the level drifts.
examples: Body warmth: temperature sensors, then the hypothalamus, then sweat glands and skin blood vessels.
A fridge: the thermostat's sensing tube, then the thermostat's switch, then the motor that pumps heat out.
A flush tank: the float, then the arm, then the inlet tap.
explanations.art: A circle of three boxes labelled sensor, control centre and effector, joined by arrows, with a fourth arrow from the effector back through 'the level' to the sensor.

explanations.concept: Closed loop or open loop: does the news come back?
explanations.definition: A closed loop checks its own result and changes its action. An open loop acts without checking.
explanations.description: To tell them apart, ask one question. Does news of the result come back and change what the system does next? A fan regulator sets a speed, and the fan keeps that speed whether the room is hot or cold. That is an open loop. An air conditioner measures the room and works harder or stops. That is a closed loop. A sensor alone does not make a closed loop. A street light with a light sensor comes on at dusk. But the lamp does not change the daylight that the sensor measures. No news about its own result comes back, so it is an open loop with a sensor. Open loops are simple and cheap, and they work well when nothing unexpected happens. Closed loops cope with disturbances, which are pushes from outside that nobody planned for. Living bodies meet disturbances all day, so they are full of closed loops.
examples: Open: a toaster timer, a washing machine's wash timer, a fan regulator, a tap left running into a bucket.
Closed: a fridge, an iron, a geyser with a thermostat, a flush tank, your pupils in bright light.
Pouring with eyes shut is open loop. Pouring while watching the level is closed loop.
explanations.art: Two drawings side by side: a tap filling a bucket that overflows with nobody watching, and a flush tank whose float has shut its tap.

explanations.concept: Set point, error and negative feedback
explanations.definition: The set point is the level a loop keeps. The error is the gap between the level now and the set point. In negative feedback, the response always acts to make the error smaller.
explanations.description: A control centre does not need to know the level itself. It needs to know the error: how far the level is from the set point, and on which side. If the level is too high, the response pushes down. If it is too low, the response pushes up. The response is opposite to the error, which is why this is called negative feedback. Why does this make things steady? Because the response shrinks the error, and a smaller error then calls for a smaller response. The loop quietens itself. There is also positive feedback, where the response makes the change bigger. A microphone held near its loudspeaker squeals for this reason. The body uses positive feedback only for things that must finish quickly, such as a blood clot sealing a cut. For keeping a level steady, it uses negative feedback.
examples: An AC set to 24 degrees in a room at 29 degrees has an error of 5 degrees, so it cools.
Blood too salty: you feel thirsty and your kidneys hold back water. Blood too watery: thirst stops and the kidneys let water go.
A float in a flush tank is below its set height, so the tap is open. As the float rises, the error shrinks to nothing and the tap shuts.
explanations.art: A horizontal dotted line labelled set point, with a wavy level line above and below it and small arrows always pointing back towards the dotted line.

explanations.concept: Delay: a loop must go round faster than the change it is correcting
explanations.definition: Every loop takes time to go round. If the change happens faster than the loop can go round, the correction arrives too late.
explanations.description: In the Stick Test, your eyes see the stick lean, your brain decides, and your arm moves the hand. One trip round takes about a fifth of a second. A pencil that starts to tip is far over in about a quarter of a second. So you get only one correction, and one is rarely enough. A stick one metre long takes more than twice as long to tip the same amount, so you can make several corrections in the time. That is why the long stick is easier, though it is bigger. Shut your eyes, and the best sensor is gone. The touch sensors in your palm still give some news, but it is rough and slow, and the stick falls. A late correction can even make things worse. If you answer where the stick was a moment ago, you may push the wrong way. Engineers call the back-and-forth swinging of a slow loop 'hunting'.
examples: A geyser takes minutes to heat, so its thermostat may be slow. A stick falls in under a second, so its loop must be very fast.
Your pupils correct for bright light in about a second. Your kidneys correct your water over an hour or more.
When the hot tap takes a few seconds to answer, people turn it too far, and then too far back.
explanations.art: A short pencil tipping over quickly beside a long stick tipping slowly, with a small clock under each showing a shorter and a longer time.

explanations.concept: Standing up: the blood pressure loop
explanations.definition: When you stand, gravity pulls blood towards your legs. Sensors in your neck arteries detect the drop in pressure, and the brainstem speeds the heart and narrows blood vessels within a few seconds.
explanations.description: Your brain needs a steady flow of blood. Blood flows because the heart keeps it under pressure. When you lie down, your head, heart and legs are at one level. When you stand, gravity pulls blood down into the legs and belly. Less blood returns to the heart, so each beat sends out less, and the pressure in the arteries of the neck starts to fall. Baroreceptors are stretch sensors in the walls of those arteries and of the large artery leaving the heart. Lower pressure stretches the walls less, so the sensors send fewer signals. Control centres in the brainstem read the change. They order the heart to beat faster and the muscle in the walls of small arteries to tighten. Pressure comes back up. All of this is finished in a few seconds, without you choosing any of it. If the loop is a little slow, you feel dizzy or your sight goes dim for a moment. Standing still, the pull of gravity continues, so the pulse stays a little faster than it was lying down.
examples: In the Stand-Up Test, most people's pulse jumps in the first 15 seconds of standing and then settles a little.
A giraffe's heart keeps the blood at about twice our pressure, because the brain is so far above the heart. Scientists are still working out how giraffes cope when they lower their heads to drink.
Astronauts back from months in orbit often feel faint when they first stand, because their loop has had no practice against gravity.
explanations.art: A child lying down and the same child standing, with the blood in the standing body drawn pulled a little towards the legs, and small sensors marked in the neck with a nerve going to the brainstem.

explanations.concept: Control centres: the brain, and cells that are their own control
explanations.definition: Many of the body's control centres are in the brainstem and the hypothalamus. But some loops have no brain part at all: one cell senses, decides and responds.
explanations.description: The brainstem runs the loops for blood pressure, heartbeat and breathing. The hypothalamus runs loops for warmth, water and hunger. In 1951 the Indian doctor Bal Krishan Anand, working with John Brobeck at Yale University, found a small area at the side of the hypothalamus in rats. When it was damaged, the rats stopped eating. The two called it a feeding centre. Later work showed that hunger is controlled by several areas and signals together, so the picture today is more complicated. Not every loop passes through the brain. A beta cell in the pancreas senses the glucose in the blood that reaches it. Glucose is the sugar your blood carries. When there is more glucose, the same cell releases more insulin, and insulin makes other cells take glucose in. The sensor and the control are inside one cell. So the saying 'the brain controls the body' is only partly true. The brain runs many loops, and many others run without it.
examples: Brainstem: blood pressure, breathing, heartbeat.
Hypothalamus: warmth, thirst, hunger.
One cell as sensor and control: a beta cell in the pancreas for glucose.
explanations.art: A body outline with the brainstem, the hypothalamus and the pancreas each marked by a small circle of arrows.

explanations.concept: Machines with loops: the float, the bending strip and the spinning balls
explanations.definition: People have built feedback loops into machines for more than two thousand years. A float valve, a thermostat and a governor each sense, compare and act.
explanations.description: About 270 BCE in Alexandria, Ktesibios built a water clock that needed a steady water level. He used a float that rose and blocked the inlet, and sank and opened it. The flush tank in a bathroom and the float valve in an overhead tank work the same way today. In an electric iron, the sensor is a bimetallic strip: two metals joined together. When heated, one metal grows longer than the other, so the strip bends. At the set temperature the bend pulls two metal contacts apart and the heater goes off. The iron cools, the strip straightens, the contacts touch and the heater comes on. The dial moves the contact, and that changes the set point. In 1788 James Watt fitted a governor to his steam engines. Two heavy balls spun with the engine. If the engine sped up, the balls swung outwards and a lever closed the steam valve a little. In each machine you can find the same three jobs as in the body. In some, one part does two jobs.
examples: Flush tank: the float is the sensor, the arm is the control, and the inlet tap is the effector.
Iron: the bimetallic strip senses, its contacts switch, and the heating coil acts.
Voltage stabiliser beside a fridge or television: it senses the mains voltage and switches its coils to correct the voltage.
explanations.art: Three small drawings in a row: a float valve in a tank, a bent two-metal strip opening a switch, and a pair of spinning balls on a steam engine.

explanations.definition: On-off control has two responses, full and none. How-much control makes the response match the size of the error.
explanations.description: An iron's heater is either on or off. So the iron heats past the set point, switches off, cools below the set point, and switches on. Its temperature moves up and down in a small zigzag. This is cheap and good enough for ironing. An older air conditioner works the same way: the compressor, which is its pump, runs fully or stops. An inverter air conditioner changes the speed of its compressor. When the room is far from the set point it runs fast, and when the room is close it runs slowly. The temperature stays smoother, and it wastes less electricity. The body mostly uses how-much control. You sweat a little when you are a little warm and a lot when you are very warm. Your heart can beat at any rate between resting and racing. But single nerve cells and muscle fibres are on-off: each one fires or does not. The body gets a how-much response by changing how many of them fire, and how often.
examples: In the Iron Light Test, the light goes on and off. The share of time it stays on is larger at a hotter setting.
In the Blind Pencil, 'left' and 'right' calls give a zigzag line. 'A little left' gives a smoother one.
Shivering can be a small tremble or a strong shake, depending on how cold you are.
explanations.art: Two graphs side by side: a sharp zigzag round a dotted line labelled on-off, and a gentle wave that settles onto the dotted line labelled how-much.

explanations.definition: A single cell runs feedback loops with molecules instead of nerves, one more kind of hardware for the same job. Molecules do the sensing, the comparing and the acting.
explanations.description: The bacterium Escherichia coli lives in the gut of humans and other animals. They swim towards food such as sugar. To do this they compare the amount of sugar now with the amount a few seconds ago. If things are getting better, they keep swimming straight. If not, they tumble and try a new direction. To compare, they must reset their sensors to each new background level. In 2000, Tau-Mu Yi, Yun Huang, Melvin Simon and John Doyle showed that this resetting is a kind of feedback that engineers already knew and used in machines, called integral feedback. Cells also control their own genes by feedback. In 1961, François Jacob and Jacques Monod showed how E. coli switch on the genes for digesting milk sugar only when milk sugar is present. So homeostasis did not begin with brains. Cells were running loops for billions of years before any animal had a nerve.
examples: E. coli reset their sugar sensors again and again, so they can detect small changes at any background level.
A cell that has made enough of a substance often uses that same substance to slow the enzyme that makes it.
The guard cells round each tiny pore in a leaf close the pore when the plant is short of water.
explanations.art: A rod-shaped bacterium with thin tails swimming towards a cloud of sugar dots, with a small circle of arrows drawn inside the cell.

explanations.concept: When a loop is broken, and how people mend it
explanations.definition: If the sensor, the control or the effector of a loop fails, the level drifts. Some broken loops can be closed again from outside.
explanations.description: In type 1 diabetes, the beta cells of the pancreas are lost, so the body's sensor and control for glucose are gone together. For a hundred years people have closed the loop by hand. They prick a finger to measure glucose, decide on a dose, and inject insulin. The person is the sensor and the control centre. Today some people wear a closed-loop system. A small sensor under the skin measures glucose every few minutes. A computer program compares the reading with a target. A pump gives more or less insulin. It is the same three jobs, done by a machine joined to a body. These systems still need the person's help at meal times, and a fully automatic one is not yet here. Other loops fail for a short time. In heatstroke the body can no longer lose heat fast enough, and the temperature climbs. A person who faints on standing has a blood pressure loop that answered too slowly. Lying flat brings the blood back to the brain.
examples: A finger-prick glucose test, a decision and an injection: a person closing a loop by hand.
A glucose sensor patch on the arm that sends readings to an insulin pump.
A helper who fans and cools a person with heatstroke is acting as that person's effector. Heatstroke needs a doctor quickly.
explanations.art: A girl with a small round sensor patch on her upper arm and a small pump clipped at her waist, with a dotted line joining the two.

explanations.concept: Is a set point really written somewhere in the body?
explanations.description: A thermostat has a dial, and the set point is a real position of that dial. Is there anything like a dial for 37 degrees in the brain? Scientists disagree. This matters because it changes how we draw the loop: one boss with a target, or many small loops with no boss.
examples: Fever: body temperature is held at a higher level for a while. One view says the dial was turned up. The other says the thresholds of the separate loops shifted.
Skin blood vessels, sweating and shivering each begin at a slightly different body temperature.

perspectives.explanation: The hypothalamus holds one set point, compares body temperature with it, and commands all the effectors, as a thermostat does.

There is no single controller and no stored number. Sweating, shivering and skin blood flow are separate loops, each with its own sensors and its own switching temperature. They seem to agree only because they all respond to the same body temperature. The steady 37 degrees is what their combined action produces.

explanations.art: A brain with a thermostat dial drawn inside it and a large question mark over the dial.

explanations.description: A thermostat acts until the room reaches 24 degrees and then stops. A bacterium swims until they reach the sugar. Both act towards an end. In 1943 Arturo Rosenblueth, Norbert Wiener and Julian Bigelow wrote that this is what purpose is: behaviour steered by negative feedback from a goal. Philosophers have argued about that ever since. A bacterium who swims towards sugar wants the sugar: every living being senses, chooses and acts. Whether the same can be said of a thermostat is a question this lesson leaves open.
examples: A dog who is hot looks for shade. A fridge that is warm runs its motor.
A float valve keeps a tank full with no wires, no brain and no program.

perspectives.who: Arturo Rosenblueth, Norbert Wiener and Julian Bigelow (1943)
perspectives.explanation: Purposeful behaviour is behaviour controlled by negative feedback from a goal. This is true of a cat chasing a mouse and of a machine that tracks a target.
That definition is too wide. A machine with feedback only behaves as if it had a purpose. Purpose needs someone who wants or intends the goal.
A bacterium's swimming is chemistry that evolution has tuned. They call it goal-directed, and they avoid the word 'want' for a single cell.

explanations.art: A thermostat dial and a swimming bacterium side by side, each with a small thought bubble holding a question mark.

explanations.concept: Does the Earth keep its own temperature steady?
explanations.description: The Sun has grown brighter over billions of years, yet the Earth has had liquid water for most of that time. Something has acted against the change. One slow loop is widely accepted. When the Earth is warmer, rain breaks down rock faster, and that takes more carbon dioxide out of the air. Less carbon dioxide means less warming. James Walker, Paul Hays and James Kasting described this in 1981. It works over hundreds of thousands of years, far too slowly to undo the warming people are causing now. A bolder idea is that living beings themselves are part of the Earth's loops.
examples: Warm, wet weather wears rock away faster than cold, dry weather does.
Daisyworld is a made-up planet in a computer. Dark daisies warm it and pale daisies cool it, and together they hold its temperature steady.

perspectives.explanation: Life and the air, sea and rocks together form one system that keeps the planet fit for life. They named it the Gaia hypothesis. Lynn Margulis supplied the knowledge of microbes that the idea needed.

Living beings do change the air and the sea, and some loops are real. But nothing shows that the whole planet is regulated for the good of life. Some changes made by living beings seem to have harmed most other life.

explanations.art: The Earth seen from space with a circle of arrows round it passing through rain, rock, sea and air.

agreed.text: Living bodies keep many inside conditions within narrow limits by negative feedback.
agreed.evidence: Claude Bernard described the steady 'inner environment' of the body in the 1860s and 1870s. Walter Cannon named homeostasis in the 1920s. Each loop since has been traced by measuring what happens when one part is blocked.

agreed.text: A feedback loop needs sensing, comparing and acting, and it fails if any of the three is missing.
agreed.evidence: You can test it yourself. In the Stick Test, closing your eyes removes the main sensor, and the stick falls within a second or two.

agreed.text: Stretch sensors in the neck arteries and the large artery from the heart report blood pressure to the brainstem.
agreed.evidence: Heinrich Hering showed the reflex from the neck artery in 1923 and found the nerve that carries the signal. Corneille Heymans received the 1938 Nobel Prize for work on these sensors.

agreed.text: A loop with a long delay tends to overshoot and swing.
agreed.evidence: Early steam engine governors made engines speed up and slow down again and again. James Clerk Maxwell explained why with mathematics in 1868, in a paper called 'On Governors'.

agreed.text: Single cells run feedback loops with molecules instead of nerves.
agreed.evidence: The loop by which E. coli reset their sugar sensors has been worked out molecule by molecule and matched to an engineer's integral feedback (Yi, Huang, Simon and Doyle, 2000).

agreed.text: The same rules of feedback describe bodies and machines.
agreed.evidence: The mathematics Maxwell wrote for governors is used today for artificial pancreas systems, aircraft autopilots and models of the blood pressure loop.

challenging.context: This card is about a common saying: that the brain controls everything in the body.
challenging.claim: The brain controls everything the body does.
challenging.for: The brainstem and hypothalamus do run the loops for blood pressure, breathing, warmth and thirst.
challenging.against: A beta cell in the pancreas senses glucose and releases insulin with no order from the brain. Kidney cells, liver cells and single bacteria run their own loops too. The brain is one control centre among many.

challenging.context: This card is about whether a stronger, quicker response always makes a loop better.
challenging.claim: The stronger the correction, the steadier the level.
challenging.for: A weak response lets the level drift a long way before it comes back.
challenging.against: A response that is too strong for the loop's delay overshoots, and the level swings from side to side. In the game Drift, Bang or Nudge, a fixed jump of 4 often lands on the far side of the target.

challenging.context: This card is about whether the body stores a target temperature the way a thermostat does.
challenging.claim: The hypothalamus holds a set point of 37 degrees, like the dial of a thermostat.
challenging.for: Body temperature behaves as if there were a dial, and fever looks like the dial being turned up.
challenging.against: Nobody has found a stored number. Andrej Romanovsky and others argue that separate loops for sweating, shivering and skin blood flow together produce the steady level.

challenging.context: This card is about whether homeostasis only reacts after something has gone wrong.
challenging.claim: The body corrects a change only after the change has happened.
challenging.for: Many responses do follow a change. Your pulse rises after you stand, not before.
challenging.against: The brain also acts ahead of time. Your mouth waters and insulin starts to rise at the sight and smell of food. Peter Sterling and Joseph Eyer named this predicting 'allostasis' in 1988.

challenging.context: This card is about the Gaia hypothesis, the idea that life helps to regulate the whole Earth.
challenging.claim: Living beings and the Earth together form one self-regulating system.
challenging.for: Life has changed the air and the oceans, and some planet-wide negative feedback loops are real.
challenging.against: Many scientists say there is no evidence that the loops act for the good of life as a whole. Some changes made by living beings have made the planet worse for most life.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find the sensors that report blood pressure? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: In the 1860s the Czech scientist Johann Czermak found that pressing a finger on the side of the neck made the heart slow down. He explained it this way. A large nerve called the vagus runs down the neck to the heart, and it slows the heart. So the finger must be squeezing that nerve. Doctors accepted this for about sixty years and called it the vagus pressure test. In 1923 the German doctor Heinrich Hering tested the idea. He showed that the slowing did not come from squeezing the vagus nerve. It began at one small spot, a slight bulge where the neck artery divides in two. Pressing or stretching the wall of that bulge slowed the heart and lowered the blood pressure. He also found the thin nerve that carries the news from that spot to the brain. The bulge held sensors. The Spanish scientist Fernando de Castro drew its nerve endings under the microscope, and Corneille Heymans of Belgium showed how they work. Heymans received the 1938 Nobel Prize. De Castro did not share it. Never press on anyone's neck to try this.
how_we_found_out.who: Johann Czermak, Heinrich Hering, Fernando de Castro and Corneille Heymans
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That pressing on the neck slows the heart because the finger squeezes the vagus nerve. Hering showed that the slowing starts from stretch sensors in the wall of the neck artery.
how_we_found_out.art: An old drawing-style picture of the side of a neck showing an artery dividing in two, with a small bulge at the fork and a thin nerve leading upwards from it.

story.title: The Post and the Cross
story.note: A made-up story. Kainakary is a real village in Kuttanad, Kerala, where many families cross the water in small boats every day. The people and the ferry are imagined. Steering by keeping a near mark and a far mark in one line is a real method that boat people use all over the world. The word 'cybernetics', the study of feedback, comes from the Greek word for a person who steers a boat.
text: Ammini had counted the river since she was seven. From their landing at Kainakary to the landing on the far bank it was forty strokes of the paddle. Her aunt Thankamma had taken the ferry canoe across more times than anyone could count. But Ammini counted. Forty strokes, with the nose of the boat pointed at the red post on the other side.

This year Thankamma let her paddle on calm mornings. Ammini sat at the back, where the steering is done, and her aunt sat in the middle with the passengers. Forty strokes. Every time, the nose of the boat touched the mud beside the red post. Ammini began to think there was nothing more to learn.
In the second week of June her aunt slipped on the wet steps and sprained her wrist. The health worker bound it with a crepe bandage and said, no paddling for ten days.
'Then who will take me across tomorrow?' the health worker asked. Her name was Sister Lissy, and three babies on the far bank were due their injections.
'Ammini will,' said Thankamma.
It rained all that night. It rained in the hills too, far to the east, where the river begins.

In the morning the water was the colour of tea with milk, and it was moving. Clumps of water hyacinth slid past the landing faster than a person walks. Sister Lissy climbed in with her blue box. Thankamma climbed in after her and sat in the middle, holding her bandaged wrist in her lap.

Ammini pointed the nose at the red post and began. One. Two. Three. She paddled well. She knew she was paddling well. The strokes were long and even, and the nose of the boat pointed at the red post the whole way.

At thirty she looked up properly, and her stomach turned over. The red post was not in front of her. It was far away to the left, and getting further. The nose still pointed towards it, but the whole boat had slid sideways down the river while she counted.

At forty the boat pushed into a mat of hyacinth below somebody's coconut grove, a long way from any landing. Sister Lissy had to climb out into mud up to her shins. She did not say anything unkind. She took off her sandals, picked up her blue box and walked up the bank.
Ammini's face was hot. 'I did forty,' she said. 'I pointed at the post. I did everything the same.'
'You did,' said her aunt. 'The river did not.'
They waited under the coconut palms. Thankamma did not explain. She watched the hyacinth go by.

When Sister Lissy came back, they dragged the boat along the bank until it was level with the far landing. Ammini's arms already ached. Across the water she could see their own landing, with its white post where the boats were tied. Behind it, quite far back, stood the church, with a small cross on the roof.
'Do you see our white post?' Thankamma asked. 'And the cross behind it?'
'Yes.'
'From here the post is right under the cross. Keep the post under the cross. That is all. Do not count.'

Ammini pushed off. She pointed the nose at the white post and paddled. After five strokes the post was no longer under the cross. It had slipped to the right of it. Only by the width of a finger, but it had moved.

She understood before she could have said it. The post had not moved. The cross had not moved. She had. The river was carrying her to one side, and the two marks were showing her so, at once, while it was still only a finger's width.

She turned the nose upstream, to the right, and pulled hard. The post crept back under the cross. She eased off. It began to slip again, so she turned the nose a little further. It was strange. The boat was not pointing at the landing at all now. It was pointing well upstream, at a clump of banana plants. But the post stayed under the cross, and the banana plants slid away to the side, and the landing grew.

In the middle of the river the current was stronger, and the post slipped faster. She gave the nose more. Near the bank the current was weak, and the post slipped the other way, to the left of the cross. She gave the nose less. She never once thought, now the current is stronger. She only watched the gap between the post and the cross, and answered it.
The boat touched the mud beside the white post. Sister Lissy stepped out with dry feet.
'How many strokes?' Thankamma asked.
Ammini opened her mouth and shut it again. She had no idea.
'Forty was right for a quiet river,' her aunt said. 'I counted it for you when you were small, on a quiet day. It was never the river's number.'

That evening the wind got up from the west and blew against the current. Ammini brought the schoolteacher home from the far bank. The post slipped to the left of the cross this time. She did not stop to wonder why. She turned the nose the other way, a little, and then a little less.
At the landing the teacher asked how long she had been steering.
'Since this morning,' Ammini said.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Ammini's count of forty strokes is a plan made in advance. It works only while nothing changes, and it has no way of noticing when something does. The post and the cross give her news of the result while she is still acting. The gap between them is the error. She turns the boat against the gap, more when the gap grows fast and less when it grows slowly. That is a feedback loop with a sensor, a comparison and a response. She does not need to know the cause of the drift, whether current or wind. She needs only to see the gap early and answer it.
ask: Why did counting forty strokes work on calm days and fail after the rain?
What did the post and the cross tell Ammini that pointing the boat at the post did not?
In the middle of the river she turned the boat more, and near the bank less. How did she know how much?
In the evening the wind pushed the boat the other way. Why did she not need a new rule?
Where in your own day do you follow a fixed plan, and where do you watch the result and correct?

printables.title: The list of loops, for every player to see
items: Each loop has four cards: Level, Sensor, Control and Effector.

rules: For 2 to 4 players. Shuffle the 32 cards. Deal 6 cards each for 2 players, or 5 each for 3 or 4 players. Hold your cards so that only you can see the fronts. Do not look at the backs.
Put the other cards in a pile with the fronts facing down on a plate or a book, so that no backs can be read. This is the pond.
On your turn, ask one player for one card. Name the job and the loop: 'Do you have the Sensor of the Flush tank loop?' You may ask only for a loop of which you already hold a card.
If that player has the card, they give it to you and you ask again. If not, they say 'Go to the pond', and you take the top card of the pond. Then the turn passes on.

When you hold all four cards of one loop, lay them down in order and read them aloud as a circle: level, sensor, control, effector, and back to the level. The others turn the cards over to check that the four backs match.
If the backs do not match, pick the cards up again and miss your next turn.
The game ends when all 8 loops are on the table. The player with the most loops wins.
To play alone: shuffle the cards, start a timer and sort them into 8 loops of four. Turn them over to check. Play again and try to beat your time.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 32 cards and the list of loops. 2. Read the 8 loop names aloud together. 3. Shuffle and deal the cards. 4. Put the rest in the pond.
flow.say: There are eight loops. Each one has a level to keep, a sensor, a control and an effector. Let's collect whole loops.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Read the eight loop names. Deal the cards. Make the pond.
flow.context: This is the first step of Loop Families. Here you cut out the cards and deal them.
flow.parent: If the card names are new, lay all 32 cards face up first and sort one loop together as an example.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to ask for a card by its job and its loop. 2. Give the card if you have it. 3. If you do not, say 'Go to the pond'. 4. Lay down each full loop and read it as a circle.

ask.q: In the Blood glucose loop, the sensor and the control are the same cells. Which loop in a machine is like that?

flow.parent: The hard part is deciding which loop a card belongs to. Let your child argue for a choice before anyone checks the back.

flow.do: 1. Count each player's loops. 2. Pick one body loop and one machine loop from the table. 3. Lay them side by side, job beside job.
flow.say: Look at these two loops side by side. What is the same about them? What is different?
flow.kid: Count your loops. Put one body loop beside one machine loop. Say what is the same.
flow.context: This is the last step of Loop Families. Here you compare a body loop with a machine loop.

check.q: Which job do the float in a flush tank and the baroreceptors in your neck share?
check.why: Both detect the level and report it. The float detects the height of the water. Baroreceptors detect how much the blood stretches the artery wall. Choosing 'effector' may mean mixing up the part that notices with the part that acts.

games.title: Drift, Bang or Nudge: which rule keeps the counter nearest to 10?
games.context: This is a dice game about three ways to control a level. A counter starts on square 10 of a number track. A die pushes it up or down each turn. You play three rounds with three different rules for pushing back, and you see which rule keeps the counter closest to 10.

printables.title: A number track, drawn as one row of squares from 0 to 20
items: Draw 21 squares in one row. Number them 0 to 20.
Colour square 10 green. This is the set point.

printables.title: Score sheet for three rounds of 12 turns
items: Round 1, Drift: no pushing back. Write the gap from 10 after each of 12 turns. Total: __
Round 2, Bang: push back by exactly 4 each turn. Write the gap from 10 after each of 12 turns. Total: __
Round 3, Nudge: push back by half the gap each turn. Write the gap from 10 after each of 12 turns. Total: __
The lowest total is the steadiest round.

rules: You need one die and one counter, such as a button or a tamarind seed. Put the counter on square 10.
Each turn starts with a disturbance. Roll the die. On 1, 2 or 3, move the counter down that many squares. On 4, 5 or 6, move the counter up 1, 2 or 3 squares.
Then push back, using the rule for the round. The counter cannot go below 0 or above 20.
Round 1, Drift: do not push back at all.
Round 2, Bang: if the counter is not on 10, move it exactly 4 squares towards 10, even if that takes it past 10.
Round 3, Nudge: count the gap between the counter and 10. Move the counter half that gap towards 10. If the gap is an odd number, round the half up. A gap of 3 means a move of 2.
After each turn, write down the gap between the counter and 10. Each round lasts 12 turns. Add up the 12 gaps.
With friends or a parent, each player plays all three rounds. The lowest total for a round wins that round. Alone, try to predict which round will have your lowest total.

setup.caption: 1. Draw the track. Put the counter on 10.

setup.art: A die showing 2 beside the track, and the button moved down from 10 to 8.
setup.caption: 2. Roll the die. Move the counter down or up.

flow.do: 1. Draw the track of 21 squares on paper and number it 0 to 20. 2. Copy the score sheet. 3. Read the three rules aloud. 4. Ask which rule will keep the counter nearest to 10, and why.
flow.say: The die is the outside world pushing the level about. Which rule do you think will hold the counter closest to 10? Why?
flow.kid: Draw the track. Read the three rules. Guess which rule is steadiest. Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of Drift, Bang or Nudge. Here you draw the track and guess which rule will win.

flow.do: 1. Play Round 1, Drift, for 12 turns. 2. Roll, move, and write the gap from 10 each turn. 3. Add up the 12 gaps.
flow.say: In this round nothing pushes back. Watch where the counter wanders.
flow.kid: Play 12 turns with no pushing back. Write the gap each turn. Add them up.
flow.context: This step of Drift, Bang or Nudge is Round 1, where nothing pushes the counter back.
flow.parent: The counter usually wanders several squares from 10 and does not come back. Sometimes it stays close by luck. That is worth noticing too.

flow.do: 1. Play Round 2, Bang, for 12 turns. 2. Play Round 3, Nudge, for 12 turns. 3. Add up the gaps for each round.
flow.say: Now you push back. In Bang you always jump 4. In Nudge you move half the gap. Watch what the counter does near 10.
flow.kid: Play Bang for 12 turns. Play Nudge for 12 turns. Add up the gaps.
flow.context: This step of Drift, Bang or Nudge is Rounds 2 and 3, where you push the counter back by two different rules.

ask.q: In Bang, the counter was 1 square from 10 and you still had to jump 4. What happened?
good: It jumped past 10 and landed 3 squares away on the other side.
The push was too big for a small gap.

flow.do: 1. Lay the three totals side by side. 2. Ask which rule was steadiest and why. 3. Ask which home machine works like Bang.
flow.say: Which total is lowest? Tell me what you saw the counter do in each round.
flow.kid: Compare your three totals. Say which rule was steadiest. Say why.
flow.context: This is the last step of Drift, Bang or Nudge. Here you compare the three rules.
flow.parent: Nudge usually wins, Bang comes second and Drift last. With only 12 turns, luck can change the order. If it does, play the round again and compare.

check.q: Why does Nudge usually keep the counter closer to 10 than Bang does?
options: Its push matches the size of the gap
check.why: Nudge makes a big move for a big gap and a small move for a small gap, so it rarely jumps past 10. Bang makes the same big move every time, so near 10 it overshoots. Choosing 'pushes harder' may mean thinking a stronger response is always better.

experiments.title: The Stick Test: which stick is easiest to balance, and what does balancing need?
experiments.context: In this experiment you balance three sticks of different lengths upright on your open palm, and a helper times each try. Then you balance the longest stick while looking at different places, and with your eyes shut. You will find out what a balancing loop needs in order to work.
experiments.question: Which is easiest to keep upright on your palm: a pencil, a 30 centimetre ruler or a stick 1 metre long? And where do your eyes need to look?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Put the pencil, the ruler and the long stick in order, from easiest to hardest to balance. Then guess which is best for the long stick: looking at its top, looking at your hand, or shutting your eyes. Write both guesses, and write the reason for each.
experiments.fair_test: In part 1, change only the stick. Use the same hand, stand in the same place and look at the top of the stick every time. In part 2, change only where you look, and keep the long stick. The helper starts the timer when your other hand lets go. The helper stops it when the stick falls off your palm or you grab it. Stop any try at 30 seconds. Do 5 tries for each stick, because one try can be lucky or unlucky.

materials.item: a pencil about 18 centimetres long
a 30 centimetre ruler
a straight stick about 1 metre long: a metre scale, a broom or mop handle, or a walking stick
a phone timer or stopwatch that shows tenths of a second
a notebook and pencil
a clear floor space about 2 metres wide, away from glass, lamps and the ceiling fan

experiments.safety: Switch off the ceiling fan. Keep the long stick away from faces, glass and shelves. The helper stands two steps back.

schedule.what: Balance three sticks, 5 tries each. Then balance the long stick while looking at three different places. Find the means and draw a bar chart.

experiments.record: Fill in the table with every try and every mean. Draw a bar chart of the three sticks, and a second bar chart for the three ways of looking. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.
