flow.say: Hold your palm flat. Stand the stick on it and let go with the other hand. You may move your hand and your feet.
flow.kid: Clear a space. Stand a stick on your flat palm. Let go. Try each stick twice.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Stick Test. Here you learn to stand a stick on your palm and you practise.
flow.parent: Moving the feet is allowed. The palm must stay open: no gripping with the fingers. Stop each try at 30 seconds.

flow.do: 1. Lay the three sticks in a row. 2. Ask your child to order them from easiest to hardest. 3. Ask for the reason. 4. Write the guess down.
flow.say: Which stick will stay up longest, and which will fall first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess which stick is easiest. Guess which is hardest. Say why. Write it down.
flow.context: This step of the Stick Test is for guessing. You guess before the timed tries.

good: The pencil is light and small, so it should be easy.
The long stick falls more slowly, so I have more time.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children and grown-ups expect the pencil to be easiest.

flow.do: 1. Your child balances the pencil 5 times, looking at its top. 2. Time each try and write it down. 3. Do the same with the ruler. 4. Do the same with the long stick.
flow.say: Look at the top of the stick every time. I will time you from the moment you let go.
flow.kid: Balance the pencil 5 times. Then the ruler. Then the long stick. Look at the top.
flow.context: This step of the Stick Test is part 1. Here you time five tries with each of the three sticks.
flow.parent: The pencil usually lasts about a second or less. Write these short times down as they are. They are a result, not a failure.

flow.do: 1. Hold up the long stick. 2. Ask which will work best: eyes on the top, eyes on the hand, or eyes shut. 3. Ask for the reason and write it down.
flow.say: Now only the long stick. Will it matter where you look? What if you shut your eyes? Why?
flow.kid: Guess where your eyes should look. Guess what shut eyes will do. Say why.
flow.context: This step of the Stick Test is the second guess. You guess how looking changes the balancing.

flow.do: 1. Use the 5 long-stick times from part 1 as 'eyes on the top'. 2. Do 5 tries looking only at the hand under the stick. 3. Do 5 tries with eyes shut, closing them just after letting go.
flow.say: This time look only at your hand, never at the top. After that, we try with your eyes shut.
flow.kid: Balance the long stick 5 times looking at your hand. Then 5 times with eyes shut.
flow.context: This step of the Stick Test is part 2. Here you change only where your eyes look.
flow.parent: Stand close during the eyes-shut tries and be ready to catch the stick. It usually falls within a second or two.

flow.do: 1. For each row, add the 5 times and divide by 5 to get the mean. 2. Draw one bar chart for the three sticks. 3. Draw a second bar chart for the three ways of looking.
flow.say: Let's find the mean of each row. Then we can see the pattern in two charts.
flow.kid: Add each row and divide by 5. Draw a bar for each stick. Draw a bar for each way of looking.
flow.context: This step of the Stick Test turns your times into means and two bar charts.

flow.do: 1. Ask what your child claims, what they saw and why they think it happened. 2. Only then read the explanation in the parent note together. 3. Write three sentences in the notebook.
flow.say: Tell me your claim, your evidence and your reason. Which stick was easiest? What did shutting your eyes do? Why?
flow.kid: Say what you found. Say what you saw. Say why you think it happened. Write three sentences.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Stick Test. Here you say and write your claim, evidence and reasoning.

ask.q: Your hand and your brain were the same with eyes shut. So what was missing?
good: The news from my eyes about which way the stick was leaning.
The sensor was missing, so the loop was broken.

ask.q: Why is the long stick easier, though it is bigger?
good: It tips over more slowly.
My eyes and hand have time for several corrections before it has gone too far.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: eyes, brain and arm make a loop that takes about a fifth of a second to go round. A pencil tips too fast for that loop. A long stick tips slowly, so there is time. With eyes shut, the main sensor is gone and the stick falls. If your long stick did not win, check that the palm stayed open and the eyes stayed on the top, then repeat.

check.q: With your eyes shut, the long stick fell quickly. Which job of the loop was missing?
check.why: Your arm could still move and your brain could still decide. But no news of the lean was coming in from your eyes, so the loop was open. Choosing 'acting' may mean thinking that balance is only about a quick hand.

experiments.title: The Stand-Up Test: what does your pulse do when you stand up?
experiments.context: In this experiment you lie still for three minutes while a helper counts your pulse. Then you stand up, and the helper counts again at once, after one minute and after two minutes. You will find out how your body keeps blood reaching your brain when you stand.
experiments.question: When you stand up after lying down, does your pulse go up, go down or stay the same? If it changes, does it stay changed?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Just after you stand up, will your pulse be faster, slower or the same as when you were lying down? What will it be two minutes later? Write your guesses and the reason for each.
experiments.fair_test: Change only one thing: lying or standing. Lie still for a full three minutes before the lying count. Stand up smoothly and then stand still, without talking or walking. The same helper counts at the same wrist each time, for 15 seconds. Do the whole test twice, because one count can be off by a beat or two.

materials.item: a bed or a mat on the floor
a clock, watch or phone that shows seconds
a notebook and pencil
a helper to count the pulse

experiments.safety: Stand up beside the bed, so that you can sit down at once if you feel dizzy or your sight goes dim. Feel the pulse only at the wrist. Never press on the neck. A child who has fainted before, or who has a heart condition, should skip this test or ask a doctor first.

schedule.what: Practise finding the pulse. Lie still for 3 minutes and count. Stand and count three times. Repeat the whole test once. Work out beats a minute and draw a line graph.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Multiply each 15-second count by 4 to get beats a minute. Draw a line graph with time along the bottom: lying, just standing, 1 minute, 2 minutes. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: pulse before and after standing up
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished graph can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A girl lying flat and relaxed on a mat on the floor while her father kneels beside her with two fingers on the inside of her wrist, below the thumb, and a phone timer in his other hand.
setup.caption: 1. Lie still for 3 minutes. A helper counts your pulse at the wrist for 15 seconds.

setup.art: The same girl standing still beside a bed with her arm held out, and her father counting the pulse at her wrist while watching the timer.
setup.caption: 2. Stand up smoothly. The helper counts at once, then after 1 minute and after 2 minutes.

flow.do: 1. Find your child's pulse on the inside of the wrist, below the thumb, using two fingers. 2. Count the beats for 15 seconds. 3. Multiply by 4. 4. Let your child find your pulse too.
flow.say: The pulse is the push of blood each time the heart beats. Let's count yours for 15 seconds and multiply by 4.
flow.kid: Find the pulse at the wrist with two fingers. Count for 15 seconds. Multiply by 4.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Stand-Up Test. Here you practise finding and counting a pulse at the wrist.
flow.parent: Press lightly with two fingers, not the thumb, because the thumb has a pulse of its own. Use the wrist only.

flow.do: 1. Explain the plan: lie down for 3 minutes, then stand. 2. Ask what the pulse will do just after standing, and 2 minutes later. 3. Ask why. 4. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: When you stand up, will your pulse be faster, slower or the same? And two minutes later? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess what your pulse will do when you stand. Say why. Write it down.
flow.context: This step of the Stand-Up Test is for guessing. You guess before you lie down.

good: Standing is a little more work, so it may go up.
Blood has to go uphill to my head when I stand.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Any reason is welcome.

flow.do: 1. Your child lies flat and still for 3 minutes, without talking. 2. In the last 15 seconds, count the pulse at the wrist. 3. Write the count beside 'Lying'.
flow.say: Lie flat and still. Breathe normally. I will count your pulse near the end of the three minutes.
flow.kid: Lie flat and still for 3 minutes. Stay quiet. Your helper counts your pulse.
flow.context: This step of the Stand-Up Test is the lying count. Here you rest for three minutes before the pulse is counted.

flow.do: 1. Keep your fingers on the wrist. 2. Your child stands up smoothly beside the bed and stands still. 3. Count for 15 seconds, starting at once. 4. Count again at 1 minute and at 2 minutes.
flow.say: Stand up now, smoothly, and stand still. I am counting straight away. Tell me if you feel dizzy.
flow.kid: Stand up smoothly and stand still. Do not talk. Your helper counts three times.
flow.context: This step of the Stand-Up Test is the standing counts. Here the pulse is counted at once, after 1 minute and after 2 minutes.
flow.parent: The first count must begin within about 5 seconds of standing, because the jump is biggest then. If your child feels dizzy, they sit down and the run ends there.

flow.do: 1. Your child lies down again for 3 minutes. 2. Repeat the lying count and the three standing counts. 3. Write them in the Run 2 columns.
flow.say: One run can be off by a beat or two. Let's do the whole thing once more and compare.
flow.kid: Lie down again for 3 minutes. Then stand. Your helper counts again.
flow.context: This step of the Stand-Up Test repeats the whole test, so that you have two runs to compare.

flow.do: 1. Multiply every count by 4. 2. Find the mean of the two runs for each time. 3. Draw the line graph. 4. Ask for the claim, the evidence and the reason before reading the parent note.
flow.say: Tell me your claim, your evidence and your reason. What did your pulse do, and why might your body do that?
flow.kid: Multiply each count by 4. Draw the graph. Say what you found, and why.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Stand-Up Test. Here you work out beats a minute and explain the result.

ask.q: Standing is not hard work. So why would the heart speed up?
good: Gravity pulls blood down towards the legs when I stand.
The heart beats faster to keep enough blood going up to the brain.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: on standing, gravity pulls blood towards the legs. Stretch sensors in the neck arteries detect the drop in pressure. The brainstem speeds the heart and tightens small arteries. Most children's pulse rises by 10 to 30 beats a minute at first, then settles a little. A rise of up to 40 has been measured in healthy children. If you found no change, the first count may have started late.

check.q: Your pulse rose when you stood up. Where are the sensors that started this response?
options: In the walls of the neck arteries
check.why: Baroreceptors in the walls of the neck arteries, and of the large artery from the heart, detect the drop in pressure. Choosing 'leg muscles' may mean thinking the pulse rose because standing is exercise.

experiments.title: The Iron Light Test: how does an iron hold its temperature?
experiments.context: In this experiment a grown-up stands an electric iron on its heel and switches it on. You watch the small indicator light and time how long it stays on and off, first at a low setting and then at a high setting. You will find out how an on-off loop holds a temperature.
experiments.question: Once an iron is hot, does its heater stay on all the time? Does the pattern change when the dial is turned to a hotter setting?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Once the iron has warmed up, will the light stay on, stay off, or go on and off? At a hotter setting, will the light be on for a larger share of the time, a smaller share or the same? Write your guesses and the reason for each.
experiments.fair_test: Change only the dial setting. Keep the iron in the same place, standing on its heel, away from the fan and from open windows. At each setting, wait until the light has gone off once before you start timing, so that the warm-up is not counted. Time two full cycles at each setting. One cycle is one 'on' and the 'off' that follows.

materials.item: an electric iron with a temperature dial and an indicator light
a heat-proof place to stand the iron on its heel, such as an ironing table or a stone kitchen counter
a phone timer or a clock that shows seconds
a notebook and pencil

experiments.safety: Only a grown-up touches the iron, the dial and the plug. The child sits at arm's length and watches the light. Afterwards the grown-up unplugs the iron and leaves it to cool for 30 minutes out of reach.

schedule.what: A grown-up runs the iron at a low setting and then a high setting. Time two on-off cycles at each. Work out the share of time the light is on.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. For each setting, add up the 'on' seconds and the 'off' seconds for the two cycles. Write the share of time on as a fraction: on seconds over total seconds. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

setup.art: An electric dry iron standing upright on its heel on an ironing table, plugged in, with its small red indicator light glowing and its dial turned to the lowest setting.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up stands the iron on its heel and switches it on at the lowest setting.

setup.art: A girl sitting at arm's length from the iron with a phone timer and a notebook, watching the indicator light, which has just gone off.
setup.caption: 2. Watch the light. Time how long it stays on and how long it stays off.

setup.art: A grown-up's hand turning the iron's dial to the cotton setting while the child waits with the timer.
setup.caption: 3. A grown-up turns the dial to a hot setting. Time two more cycles.

flow.do: 1. Stand the iron on its heel on a heat-proof surface. 2. Turn the dial to the lowest fabric setting. 3. Before plugging in, ask for both guesses and the reasons. 4. Write them down.
flow.say: When the iron is hot, will the light stay on, stay off, or go on and off? What will a hotter setting change? Why?
flow.kid: Guess what the light will do. Guess what a hotter setting changes. Say why.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Iron Light Test. Here a grown-up sets up the iron and you guess.
flow.parent: A steam iron works too, with no water in it. If your iron has no light, listen for the click of its switch instead.

flow.do: 1. Plug in and switch on. 2. Wait until the light goes off for the first time. 3. From then, time each 'on' and each 'off' for two full cycles. 4. Write the seconds in the table.
flow.say: The first warm-up does not count. When the light goes off, we wait. Tell me the moment it comes back on.
flow.kid: Wait for the light to go off once. Then time each 'on' and each 'off'. Do two cycles.
flow.context: This step of the Iron Light Test times the light at the lowest setting.
flow.parent: At a low setting the light may stay off for several minutes and come on for under half a minute. If two cycles take more than 10 minutes, time one cycle and say so in the table.

flow.do: 1. Turn the dial to the cotton setting. 2. Wait until the light has gone off once at this setting. 3. Time two full cycles. 4. Unplug the iron and leave it to cool out of reach.
flow.say: I am turning the dial to a hotter setting. That moves the set point. Watch what happens to the 'on' times and the 'off' times.
flow.kid: A grown-up turns the dial up. Wait for the light to go off once. Time two cycles.
flow.context: This step of the Iron Light Test times the light at a hot setting.

flow.do: 1. For each setting, add the 'on' seconds and the 'off' seconds. 2. Write the share of time on as a fraction. 3. Ask for the claim, the evidence and the reason. 4. Then read the parent note together.
flow.say: At which setting was the light on for a larger share of the time? Why would a hotter iron need that?
flow.kid: Add the 'on' times and the 'off' times. Write the fraction. Say what you found, and why.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Iron Light Test. Here you compare the two settings and explain the pattern.

ask.q: The heater is either fully on or fully off. So how does the iron manage to be hotter at one setting than another?
good: The switch stays closed until the iron is hotter.
The heater is on for a bigger share of the time.

flow.parent: After your child has answered: a bimetallic strip inside bends as it heats and opens the switch at the set temperature. The iron cools, the strip straightens and the switch closes. A hotter iron loses heat to the room faster, so the heater must be on for a larger share of the time. Irons differ a great deal, so write down what yours did.

check.q: What does turning the iron's dial change?
options: The temperature at which the switch opens
check.why: The dial moves the switch contact, so the strip must bend further, at a higher temperature, before the switch opens. The heater's strength stays the same. Choosing 'how strongly' may mean thinking of the dial as a fan regulator.

activities.title: Pour to the Line: eyes open, eyes shut, finger in
activities.context: In this activity you pour water into a tumbler up to a line, three times. First you watch, then you shut your eyes, and then you shut your eyes with one fingertip inside the rim. You will find out what your hand needs in order to stop at the right moment.

materials.item: a clear glass tumbler, or a clear plastic bottle cut down by a grown-up
a rubber band or a marker pen, to make a line about 2 centimetres below the rim
a jug or lota with about 1 litre of cool water
a large tray, or do it at the sink
a ruler, and a scarf to cover the eyes

activities.safety: Use cool water only. Never try the finger method with a hot drink until a grown-up has shown you how.
activities.record: Write down the gap between the water and the line for each of the three ways, in millimetres. Write 'over' if the water went above the line.

setup.art: A clear glass tumbler with a rubber band round it about two centimetres below the rim, standing on a steel tray, and a child pouring water into it from a small jug while watching the level.
setup.caption: 1. Mark a line 2 centimetres below the rim. Pour to the line with your eyes open.

setup.art: The same child with a scarf tied over the eyes, pouring from the jug into the tumbler on the tray, with water just spilling over the rim.
setup.caption: 2. Cover your eyes. Pour again and stop where you think the line is.

setup.art: The child with eyes covered, one fingertip hooked over the rim of the tumbler so that the tip is at the rubber band, pouring slowly with the other hand.
setup.caption: 3. Eyes still covered, hook one fingertip over the rim. Pour until the water touches it.

flow.do: 1. Stand the tumbler on the tray. 2. Put the rubber band 2 centimetres below the rim. 3. Your child pours to the line with eyes open. 4. Measure the gap between water and line.
flow.say: Pour the water up to the line and stop. Then we will measure how close you got.
flow.kid: Pour water up to the line. Stop. Measure the gap with the ruler.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pour to the Line. Here you pour with your eyes open.

ask.q: How did your hand know when to stop?
good: I watched the water come up to the line.
My eyes told me.

flow.do: 1. Empty the tumbler into the jug. 2. Ask whether your child will get as close with eyes covered, and why. 3. Cover the eyes. 4. Your child pours and stops. Measure the gap.
flow.say: Now with your eyes covered. Will you get as close as before? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how close you will get with eyes shut. Say why. Pour. Measure the gap.
flow.context: This step of Pour to the Line is the pour with your eyes covered.
flow.parent: Most children stop far too early or pour over the rim. A few listen to the sound of the water, which rises in pitch as the tumbler fills. If your child does this, say that the ears became the sensor.

flow.do: 1. Empty the tumbler again. 2. Eyes still covered, your child hooks one fingertip over the rim, down to the line. 3. Your child pours slowly until the water touches the finger. 4. Measure the gap and compare all three.
flow.say: Keep your eyes covered. Put one fingertip inside the rim, down at the line. Pour slowly, and stop when you feel the water.
flow.kid: Hook one fingertip over the rim. Pour slowly. Stop when water touches your finger.
flow.context: This is the last step of Pour to the Line. Here you pour with eyes covered and a fingertip at the line.

ask.q: Your eyes were covered both times. Why was the third pour so much better than the second?
good: My finger told me when the water reached the line.
News about the level came back to me, so I could stop.

flow.parent: News of the result that comes back and changes the action is called feedback. Many people who cannot see pour tea in exactly this way.

check.q: With eyes covered and no finger in the tumbler, the pour went wrong. Why?
options: No news of the water level came back
check.why: The hand could pour and stop just as well. But nothing told it where the water was, so it could not stop at the right moment. Choosing 'weaker' may mean thinking that control is only about the part that acts.

activities.title: Open or Closed? A loop hunt round the home
activities.context: In this activity you walk round your home and look at eight machines. For each one you ask whether it checks its own result. You will sort them into closed loops and open loops, and find the sensor, the control and the effector in the closed ones.

materials.item: paper slips or sticky notes in two colours
a pencil and a notebook

activities.safety: Look and listen only. A grown-up opens the lid of a flush tank or touches anything hot or plugged in.
activities.record: Make a table with five columns: the machine, open or closed, its sensor, its control and its effector. Fill in the last three columns only for closed loops.

setup.art: A girl with a notebook standing in a kitchen and pointing at a fridge, with a pressure cooker on the stove and a mixer-grinder on the counter.
setup.caption: 1. Choose eight machines at home. For each one ask: does it check its own result?

setup.art: A mother holding the lid of a flush tank while the girl looks inside at a ball float on an arm.
setup.caption: 2. With a grown-up, look inside a flush tank. Find the float, the arm and the tap.

setup.art: A yellow sticky note on a fridge reading 'closed' and a blue one on a ceiling fan regulator reading 'open'.
setup.caption: 3. Label each machine 'closed' or 'open'.

flow.do: 1. Together, list eight machines in your home. 2. Include a fan with a regulator, a fridge, an iron and a mixer-grinder. 3. Add a flush tank, a geyser, a pressure cooker and a tube light, or whatever you have.
flow.say: For each machine we ask one question. Does news of its result come back and change what it does?
flow.kid: List eight machines at home. For each one ask: does it check its own result?
flow.context: This is the first step of Open or Closed? Here you choose eight machines to look at.

flow.do: 1. Visit each machine. 2. Your child says 'open' or 'closed' and gives a reason. 3. Stick a note on it. 4. A grown-up lifts the flush tank lid so that you can both watch one flush and refill.
flow.say: The fan turns at the speed we set. If the room gets colder, does the fan slow down by itself? What about the fridge?
flow.kid: Go to each machine. Say 'open' or 'closed'. Say why. Stick a note on it.
flow.context: This step of Open or Closed? is the hunt. Here you decide for each machine and label it.

ask.q: A pressure cooker's weight lifts and lets steam out when the pressure is too high. Open or closed?
good: Closed. The pressure itself lifts the weight, and letting steam out lowers the pressure.
The weight is the sensor and the effector together.

flow.parent: Open loops: a fan regulator, a mixer-grinder, a tube light, a toaster or washing machine timer. Closed loops: a fridge, an iron, a geyser with a thermostat, a flush tank, a pressure cooker, an air conditioner. A motor that fills the overhead tank is open if a person switches it off, and closed if a float switch does.

flow.do: 1. Choose three closed loops. 2. For each, find the sensor, the control and the effector. 3. Write them in the table. 4. Ask about a street light that comes on at dusk.
flow.say: A street light has a light sensor and comes on at dusk. Is it a closed loop? Think about what the sensor measures.
flow.kid: Pick three closed loops. Find the sensor, the control and the effector in each.
flow.context: This is the last step of Open or Closed? Here you find the three jobs inside three closed loops.
flow.parent: The street light is a trap. Its sensor measures daylight, and the lamp does not change the daylight. No news of its own result comes back, so it is an open loop with a sensor.

check.q: Which question tells you whether a machine is a closed loop?
options: Does news of its result change its action?
check.why: A closed loop measures its own result and changes what it does. A sensor alone is not enough: a dusk street light has a sensor but never checks its own effect. Choosing 'has a sensor' is the most common mix-up.

activities.title: The Blind Pencil: 'left' and 'right', or 'a little left'?
activities.context: In this activity one person draws along a winding road on paper with eyes shut. A second person is the eyes. You try three ways: no help, help with only the words 'left' and 'right', and help that says how much. You will find out how the kind of message changes the path.

materials.item: plain A4 paper
a pencil and two colour pencils
a scarf to cover the eyes
a second person to be the eyes

activities.record: For each of the three rounds, count how many times the pencil line crossed an edge of the road. Write the three counts side by side.

setup.art: A sheet of A4 paper with a winding road drawn across it from one short edge to the other, made of two wavy lines about three centimetres apart.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a winding road across the paper, two finger-widths wide. Make three copies.

setup.art: Two girls sitting side by side at a table, one with a scarf over her eyes drawing along the road with a pencil, the other watching the pencil closely and speaking.
setup.caption: 2. The driver covers their eyes and draws. The other person is the eyes.

setup.art: Three finished sheets side by side: one with a line wandering right off the road, one with a sharp zigzag between the road's edges, and one with a smooth line down the middle.
setup.caption: 3. Count how many times each line crossed the edge of the road.

flow.do: 1. Draw the same winding road on three sheets: two lines about 3 centimetres apart, with four bends. 2. Sit side by side. 3. The driver studies the first road for 10 seconds, then covers their eyes and draws along it with no help.
flow.say: Look at the road for ten seconds. Now cover your eyes and draw along it from memory. I will say nothing.
flow.kid: Look at the road for 10 seconds. Cover your eyes. Draw along it from memory.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Blind Pencil. Here the driver draws with no help at all.
flow.parent: Hold the paper still for the driver. This round is an open loop: a plan made in advance, with no news coming back.

flow.do: 1. Take the second sheet. 2. Ask which will be better: 'left' and 'right' only, or messages that say how much. Ask why. 3. The driver draws again. The eyes may say only 'left' or 'right', and only when the pencil touches an edge.
flow.say: This time I may say only 'left' or 'right', and only when you touch an edge. What do you think your line will look like? Why?
flow.kid: Guess what your line will look like. Say why. Draw again. Listen for 'left' or 'right'.
flow.context: This step of the Blind Pencil is the round with only two messages, 'left' and 'right'.
flow.parent: Agree on left and right from the driver's side before you start. The line usually zigzags from edge to edge.

flow.do: 1. Take the third sheet. 2. The driver draws again. 3. The eyes may speak at any time, and say how much: 'a little left', 'a lot right', 'straight'.
flow.say: Now I can talk all the time, and I can say how much. Go slowly.
flow.kid: Draw again. This time the eyes say how much: 'a little left', 'a lot right'.
flow.context: This step of the Blind Pencil is the round with messages that say how much.

flow.do: 1. Lay the three sheets side by side. 2. Count the edge crossings on each. 3. Ask what made the difference. 4. Swap roles if there is time.
flow.say: Look at the three lines. What was different about the messages each time? Which line is most like an iron's temperature?
flow.kid: Count the crossings on each sheet. Say what made the difference.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Blind Pencil. Here you compare the three lines.

ask.q: In round 2 the messages came only at the edge. In round 3 they came early. What did that change?
good: In round 3 I could correct before I reached the edge.
Early, small corrections kept the line near the middle.

check.q: The 'left' and 'right' round gave a zigzag line. Which machine controls its level in the same way?
options: An iron with an on-off switch
check.why: An iron's heater is fully on or fully off, so its temperature zigzags round the set point, as the pencil did between the road's edges. An inverter air conditioner changes how hard it works, like the 'a little left' messages. A fan regulator has no feedback at all.

projects.title: The Bowl That Refills Itself: a three-day water loop
projects.context: In this three-day project you make a water bowl that keeps its own level, using a bottle with one small hole. You put it on a window sill or balcony beside a plain plate of water with no bottle. Each morning and evening you measure both. You will find out how a loop can work with no brain and no wires.

materials.item: a clear 1 litre plastic bottle with a cap that closes tightly
steel plates with a rim at least 2 centimetres high, both the same size
a nail or the point of a pair of scissors, for a grown-up to make the hole
a marker pen and a ruler
a window sill, balcony or terrace corner where the plates can stay for 3 days

projects.safety: A grown-up makes the hole in the bottle. After three days, empty both plates and scrub them, because mosquitoes lay eggs in standing water. If you keep the bowl for birds, change the water and scrub the plate every two days.

schedule.what: Make the hole. Fill the bottle and stand it in one plate. Fill the plain plate to the same depth. Mark and measure everything.
Morning and evening, measure the water depth in both plates and the water level in the bottle.
Measure once more. Draw a line graph of the three levels. Explain where the loop's sensor and effector are. Empty and scrub the plates.

projects.record: Make a table with four columns: day and time, depth in the bottle plate in millimetres, depth in the plain plate in millimetres, and height of water in the bottle in centimetres. On day 3, draw all three as lines on one graph.

setup.art: A clear plastic bottle standing upright with a small round hole in its side one centimetre above the base, and a grown-up's hand holding a nail beside it.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up makes one hole, as wide as a pencil, 1 centimetre above the base of the bottle.

setup.art: The capped bottle full of water standing in a steel plate, with water in the plate just covering the hole and a single air bubble rising inside the bottle.
setup.caption: 2. Fill the bottle, cap it tightly and stand it in a plate. Water runs out until it covers the hole.

setup.art: Two steel plates of water on a balcony ledge, one with the bottle standing in it and one plain, with a ruler standing in the plain plate and a sparrow perched on the rim.
setup.caption: 3. Put a plain plate of water beside it. Measure both every morning and evening.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up makes a hole as wide as a pencil, 1 centimetre above the base of the bottle. 2. Cover the hole with a finger and fill the bottle to the top. 3. Screw the cap on tightly. 4. Stand the bottle in a plate and take the finger away.
flow.say: Watch the hole and the plate. What happens to the water? When does it stop?
flow.kid: Fill the bottle with a finger on the hole. Cap it tightly. Stand it in the plate. Watch.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bowl That Refills Itself, on day 1. Here you make the bottle and watch it fill the plate.
flow.parent: Water runs out and air bubbles in until the water in the plate covers the hole. Then it stops. If it does not stop, the cap is leaking air: tighten it. The rim of the plate must be higher than the top of the hole.

flow.do: 1. Ask what will happen if you take two spoonfuls of water out of the plate, and why. 2. Take them out and watch. 3. Pour water into the plain plate to the same depth. 4. Measure both depths.
flow.say: If I spoon some water out of this plate, what will the bottle do? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess what happens if you spoon water out. Say why. Try it. Watch for bubbles.
flow.context: This step of the Bowl That Refills Itself tests the bowl by taking water out, on day 1.

ask.q: What told the bottle to let more water out?
good: The water in the plate dropped below the top of the hole.
Air could get in through the hole, so water could come out.

flow.parent: When the level drops below the top of the hole, a bubble of air slips in and some water comes out. The level rises, covers the hole and the flow stops.

flow.do: 1. Carry both plates to a window sill or balcony. 2. Mark the water level on the bottle with the marker and write the time. 3. Ask what each plate will look like in 3 days, and why. 4. Write the guess down.
flow.say: Sun, wind and perhaps birds will take water from both plates. What will each one look like in three days? Why?
flow.kid: Put both plates outside. Mark the bottle's level. Guess what each plate will do. Say why.
flow.context: This step of the Bowl That Refills Itself sets both plates outside and records your guess, on day 1.

flow.do: 1. Each morning and evening, measure the depth of water in both plates at the same spot. 2. Measure the height of the water in the bottle. 3. Write the readings in the table.
flow.say: Let's measure both plates and the bottle. Which numbers are changing, and which are staying the same?
flow.kid: Measure both plates and the bottle. Write the numbers in your table.
flow.context: This step of the Bowl That Refills Itself is the measuring on day 2.
flow.wait: Do this on day 2, morning and evening
flow.parent: In hot, dry weather the plain plate may be dry within two days. In the monsoon, rain can fill both plates. Then move them under cover and start again. On a hot afternoon the bottle plate may stand a millimetre or two higher, because the air in the bottle warms, swells and pushes a little water out.

flow.do: 1. Take the last readings. 2. Draw one graph with three lines: bottle plate, plain plate and bottle. 3. Ask for the claim, the evidence and the reason. 4. Ask where the sensor, the control and the effector are. 5. Empty and scrub both plates.
flow.say: Which level stayed steady, and which level paid for it? Where is this loop's sensor? Is there a control centre?
flow.kid: Draw three lines on one graph. Say which level stayed steady. Find the sensor.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Bowl That Refills Itself, on day 3. Here you draw the graph and explain the loop.

ask.q: The plate with the bottle stayed at one depth. Where did the water that dried up come from?
good: From the bottle. Its level went down each day.
The bottle is a store that the loop draws on.

flow.parent: The water surface at the hole is the sensor. The air bubble and the water that follows are the response. No separate part compares or decides, yet the level is held. The loop will fail when the bottle is empty.

check.q: What will happen to the level in the bottle plate when the bottle runs empty?
options: It will stay steady for ever
It will start to fall, like the plain plate
check.why: The loop keeps the plate's level by drawing on a store. When the store is gone, nothing replaces the lost water, and the level drifts. Choosing 'stay steady' may mean forgetting that keeping a level steady always uses something up.

challenges.title: The Tumbler That Tells You: fill it to the line without looking or touching
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. In Pour to the Line, you stopped at the line with your eyes shut by keeping a fingertip in the water. That will not do for hot tea. Here you build something that brings news of the level to your hand or your ears.
challenges.problem: With your eyes covered, pour water into a steel tumbler and stop within 1 centimetre of a line inside it. Do it three times in a row. No part of your body may touch the water.
constraints: The eyes stay covered from before the pour until after it stops.
No finger or other body part may touch the water. Imagine that it is hot.
Nobody else may tell you when to stop.
Use only things from the house.
materials: a steel tumbler and a jug of cool water
drinking straws, plastic bottle caps and small bits of thermocol or cork
thick paper or card, tape, thread and rubber bands
a steel spoon, paper clips and two paper cups
general: Make a float with a mast. Tape a straw upright in a bottle cap. Cover the tumbler with a card that has a small hole for the straw and a gap for pouring. Hold a finger above the straw and stop when the straw touches it.
Listen. The sound of pouring water rises in pitch as the tumbler fills. Practise until you know the sound at the line.
Pour from a small cup that holds exactly the right amount, measured beforehand with eyes open.
creative: Use weight as the sensor. Balance a ruler across a pencil, with the tumbler on one end and a tumbler already filled to the line on the other. Stop when your end goes down.
Make a spillway. Use a paper cup with a small hole at the line, standing inside a bowl. Stop when you hear water trickle from the hole.
Let the float ring a bell. As the straw mast rises, it lifts a paper clip until the clip tips a spoon that clinks on the tumbler.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own. Test it three times with your eyes covered. Then name its sensor. Is the loop closed by your device alone, or by your device and you together?

setup.art: A steel tumbler on a tray with a pencil line inside it two centimetres below the rim, a jug of water, straws, bottle caps, card and tape laid out beside it.
setup.caption: 1. Mark a line inside a steel tumbler. Collect straws, caps, card and tape.

setup.art: A steel tumbler covered by a card with a drinking straw poking up through a small hole, the straw taped to a bottle cap floating inside, and a child with covered eyes holding a finger just above the straw while pouring.
setup.caption: 2. Build something that brings news of the level to your hand or ears. Test it with your eyes covered.

flow.do: 1. Mark a line inside the tumbler, 2 centimetres below the rim. 2. Your child pours once with eyes covered and nothing else. 3. Measure the gap. 4. Read the problem and its limits aloud.
flow.say: That is how close you get with no news coming back. Now you may build anything that brings you the news without touching the water.
flow.kid: Pour once with eyes covered. Measure the gap. Read the rules of the challenge.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Tumbler That Tells You. Here you see how the pour goes with no feedback.

flow.do: 1. Look at the usual ideas: a float with a mast, listening, or a measured cup. 2. Your child chooses one and says why it should work. 3. Build it and test it three times with eyes covered.
flow.say: Which of these would you trust? What is the sensor in it? Build it and try three pours.
flow.kid: Pick one idea. Say what its sensor is. Build it. Test it three times.
flow.context: This step of the Tumbler That Tells You tries one of the usual ideas.

ask.q: The measured cup works with no sensor at all. When would it fail?
good: If the tumbler already had some water in it.
If I spilt some. It is an open loop, so it cannot notice a change.

flow.parent: A bottle-cap float tips over easily. The hole in the card keeps the straw upright. Expect to rebuild it once or twice.

flow.do: 1. Read the creative ideas. 2. Your child designs their own, draws it and builds it. 3. Test it three times with eyes covered. 4. Name the sensor and say who closes the loop.
flow.say: Now your own design. What will sense the level? How will the news reach you?
flow.kid: Design your own. Draw it and build it. Test it three times. Name its sensor.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Tumbler That Tells You. Here you design, build and test your own idea.

check.q: A float with a mast tells your finger when the tumbler is full. Who is the effector in this loop?
check.why: The float is the sensor and the straw carries the news. Your hand is the part that acts, by tipping the jug or stopping. The device and you together make one closed loop.

challenges.title: The Short Stick Problem: make a pencil stay up for 10 seconds
challenges.context: This is an engineering challenge. In the Stick Test, a pencil stood on your palm fell in about a second, because it tips faster than your loop can go round. Here you change the pencil so that it stays up for 10 seconds.
challenges.problem: Make a pencil stay upright on your palm or on one fingertip for 10 seconds. You may add things to the pencil. You may not hold it with the other hand.
constraints: The pencil must stand on your palm or fingertip, touching nothing else.
Nothing may be stuck to your hand.
Whatever you add must come from the house.
materials: a small potato or a ball of stiff atta dough
two steel forks, or two more pencils and four clothes pegs
general: Tape the pencil to the top of a ruler, so that together they make a longer stick, and balance that.
Put a lump of dough on the top of the pencil. A heavier top tips a little more slowly.
Stand the pencil in a wide, flat lump of dough, so that it has a broad base.
creative: Push the pencil through a small potato near its point. Stick two forks into the potato so that their handles hang down and outwards, lower than the pencil point. Rest the point on one fingertip.
Use two more pencils in place of the forks. Push them into the potato slanting downwards, and clip two clothes pegs on the end of each.
Spin it. Push the pencil through the centre of a card disc and spin it like a top on a steel plate held on your palm. It stays upright while it spins fast, though it may not last 10 seconds.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own. Then test every design with your eyes shut. Which ones still stay up? Those designs need no loop from you. What is different about them?

setup.art: A pencil lying fallen on an open palm, beside a small potato, two steel forks, a ball of dough, a ruler and tape on a table.
setup.caption: 1. A bare pencil falls at once. Collect a potato or dough, two forks, a ruler and tape.

setup.art: A pencil pushed through a small potato near its point, with two forks stuck into the potato and hanging down and outwards on either side, the pencil point resting on a child's fingertip and standing upright.
setup.caption: 2. Change the pencil so that it stays up for 10 seconds. Then test it with your eyes shut.

flow.do: 1. Your child balances the bare pencil on a palm three times. 2. Time each try and write it down. 3. Read the problem and its limits aloud.
flow.say: This is the time to beat. Why did the pencil fall so fast in the Stick Test?
flow.kid: Balance the bare pencil three times. Write the times. Read the challenge.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Short Stick Problem. Here you time the bare pencil.

ask.q: Why did the pencil fall so fast?
good: A short stick tips over faster than a long one.
My eyes and hand need about a fifth of a second, and the pencil does not wait.

flow.do: 1. Look at the usual ideas: a longer stick, a heavy top or a broad base. 2. Your child chooses one and says why it should work. 3. Build it and time it three times.
flow.say: Which idea gives your loop more time? Which idea needs no loop at all? Build one and test it.
flow.kid: Pick one idea. Say why it should work. Build it. Time it three times.
flow.context: This step of the Short Stick Problem tries one of the usual ideas.

flow.do: 1. Build the potato-and-forks design, or your child's own. 2. Time it three times. 3. Test every design again with eyes shut. 4. Sort the designs into 'needs my loop' and 'steady without me'.
flow.say: Now shut your eyes with each design. Which ones stay up without any help from your eyes?
flow.kid: Build your own design. Time it. Then test each design with eyes shut.
flow.context: This is the last step of the Short Stick Problem. Here you find which designs stay up with no loop.
flow.parent: With the forks hanging lower than the fingertip, most of the weight is below the point of support. A small lean then swings back by itself, as a hanging thing does. The longer stick and the heavy top still need the eyes.

check.q: The pencil with hanging forks stayed up even with eyes shut. Why did that design need no feedback loop?
options: Its weight hangs below the support
check.why: When the weight is below the point of support, a lean swings back by itself. Nothing has to sense and correct. A bare pencil has its weight above the support, so every lean grows, and only a loop can save it. Choosing 'heavier' misses where the weight is.

worksheets.title: Feedback loops: sensor, control and effector (core)

items.p: Which three jobs does every feedback loop need?
items.why: A loop must detect the change, compare it with what is needed, and act. Take one away and the level drifts.

items.p: The part of a loop that detects a change is called the ____.
items.why: A sensor detects one kind of change and reports it. In the body a sensor is also called a receptor.

items.p: Match each part of the body-warmth loop to its job.
items.why: The nerve endings detect warmth. The hypothalamus compares and sends an order. The sweat glands carry it out, and what they do is the response.

items.p: True or false: a fan with a regulator slows down by itself when the room gets cold.
items.why: False. A fan regulator sets a speed and never checks the room. It is an open loop.

items.p: Sort each machine: closed loop or open loop?
items.why: A fridge, an iron and a flush tank each measure their own result and change what they do. The others run as set, whatever the result.

items.p: You pour water with your eyes shut and it overflows. What was missing?
items.why: With eyes shut, no news of the level came back, so the hand could not stop in time. The loop was open.

items.p: In the Stick Test, the pencil fell much sooner than the long stick. Explain why.
items.a: A short stick tips over faster than a long one. My eyes, brain and hand need about a fifth of a second for each correction. The pencil is too far over before the correction arrives. The long stick tips slowly, so there is time for several corrections.
items.why: A strong answer compares two times: how fast the stick tips, and how long the loop takes to go round.

items.p: With eyes shut, the long stick fell quickly. Which part of the loop had been removed?
items.why: The eyes are the main sensor for the stick's lean. The brain and the arm were unchanged.

items.p: Put these in order, for what happens when you stand up.
a: Gravity pulls blood towards your legs
Pressure in the neck arteries falls a little
The brainstem speeds the heart and tightens small arteries
items.why: The fall in pressure is sensed in the neck arteries. The brainstem compares and orders the heart and arteries to act. The response undoes the fall.

items.p: Stretch sensors in the walls of the neck arteries are called ____.
items.why: Baroreceptors report how much the blood is stretching the artery wall, which shows the pressure.

items.p: Match each part of a flush tank to its job in the loop.
items.why: The float detects the height. The arm turns that height into more or less opening. The tap lets water in.

items.p: What does the bimetallic strip in an iron do when it gets hot?
opts: It bends and opens a switch
items.why: The strip is two metals joined together. One grows more when heated, so the strip bends, and the bend pulls the switch open.

items.p: Draw the loop for a fridge as a circle. Label the sensor, the control, the effector and the level.
items.a: A circle of four parts with arrows: the temperature inside the fridge, the thermostat's sensor, the thermostat switch, and the compressor motor, which leads back to the temperature.
items.why: A strong drawing is a closed circle. The arrow from the motor must come back to the temperature, because the motor's work changes what the sensor detects.

items.p: True or false: an iron's heater is on for a larger share of the time at a hotter setting.
items.why: True. A hotter iron loses heat to the room faster, so the heater must be on for more of the time to make up the loss.

items.p: A street light has a light sensor and comes on at dusk. Is it a closed loop? Give your reason.
items.a: No. The sensor measures daylight, and the lamp does not change the daylight. No news about the lamp's own result comes back, so the loop is open.
items.why: A strong answer says that a sensor alone is not enough. The result of the action must come back to the sensor.

worksheets.title: Error, delay and two kinds of control (stretch)

items.p: In a loop, what does 'error' mean?
opts: A mistake made by the sensor
The gap between level and set point
items.why: The error is how far the level is from the set point, and on which side. It is a measurement, not a mistake.

items.p: Feedback that acts against a change is called ____ feedback.
items.why: 'Negative' here means opposite. The response pushes the level back the opposite way to the change.

items.p: An AC is set to 24 degrees. The room is at 30 degrees. What is the error?
items.why: The error is the gap between now and the set point. 30 − 24 = 6, and the room is on the warm side.

items.p: Sort each control: on-off, or how-much?
items: a fridge motor that runs or stops
items.why: On-off parts have two states. How-much parts can give a small, medium or large response to match the error.

items.p: In Drift, Bang or Nudge, the Bang rule always jumps 4 squares. Why does it overshoot near 10?
items.a: Near 10 the gap is only 1 or 2 squares. A jump of 4 is bigger than the gap, so the counter lands on the far side of 10. The response does not match the size of the error.
items.why: A strong answer compares the size of the push with the size of the gap.

items.p: A pencil tips in 0.25 seconds. Your loop takes 0.2 seconds. How many corrections can you make?
items.why: A fifth of a second is 0.2 seconds and a quarter is 0.25 seconds. Only one trip round the loop fits in that time, and one correction is rarely enough.

items.p: True or false: making a correction stronger always makes a level steadier.
items.why: False. A correction that is too strong for the loop's delay overshoots, and the level swings from side to side.

items.p: Put these in order, for one on-off cycle of a hot iron.
a: The iron cools below the set temperature
The strip straightens and the switch closes
The heater warms the base plate
The strip bends and the switch opens
items.why: Cooling closes the switch, and heating opens it again. The temperature moves up and down round the set point.

items.p: Match each loop to its control centre.
items.why: The brainstem and hypothalamus are in the brain. Beta cells sense and decide for themselves. In a fridge, the thermostat switch decides.

items.p: While you keep standing, your pulse stays a little faster than it was lying down. Why?
items.a: Gravity keeps pulling blood towards the legs for as long as I stand. The disturbance has not gone away, so the response must continue to hold the pressure up.
items.why: A strong answer says that the disturbance continues, so the response continues.

items.p: A beta cell senses glucose and releases insulin. Which jobs of the loop does this one cell do?
items.why: The beta cell detects glucose and decides how much insulin to release. Liver, muscle and fat cells are the effectors.

items.p: True or false: a single bacterium can run a feedback loop.
items.why: True. E. coli reset their sugar sensors by a feedback loop made of molecules. No nerves are needed.

items.p: Draw what happens to the temperature of an iron over ten minutes. Add a dotted line for the set point.
items.a: A zigzag line that rises above a dotted horizontal line, falls below it, and rises again, several times.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the temperature crossing the set point both ways. With an on-off heater it cannot sit exactly on the line.

items.p: Two girls are talking about the bowl that refills itself from a bottle with a hole.

views.who: Yamuna, a girl in Class 5 (an imagined view)
views.says: It is not a real feedback loop. It has no control centre. Nothing in it compares or decides.

views.who: Shalini, a girl in Class 5 (an imagined view)
views.says: It is a real loop. The falling level lets air in, and that brings the level back. News of the result changes the action.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with more? What did you see in this lesson that supports it?
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side and gives evidence. For Shalini: the level came back each time water was taken out. For Yamuna: there is no separate part that compares the level with a target.
items.why: Both girls are using the science. The answer depends on whether a loop needs three separate parts or only needs the result to come back and change the action. Engineers accept the second.

items.p: The self-filling bowl keeps its level only while its store lasts. The store is the water in the ____.
items.why: The plate's level stays the same while the bottle's level falls. When the bottle is empty, the plate begins to dry.

worksheets.title: Loops in cells, machines and the Earth (challenge)

items.p: Design a loop that keeps a fish tank at 26 degrees. Name its sensor, its control and its effector.
items.a: Sensor: a thermometer part in the water that reports the temperature. Control: a switch that compares the temperature with 26 degrees. Effector: a small heater in the water, switched on when the water is below 26 and off when it is above.
items.why: A strong answer names all three jobs and says which way the effector acts when the water is too cold.

items.p: A loop's news arrives 5 seconds late, and the level can change a lot in 1 second. What is likely?
opts: The level swings back and forth
items.why: The loop answers where the level was 5 seconds ago. By then the level has moved on, so the correction is often wrong and the level swings.

items.p: True or false: every loop in the human body has its control centre in the brain.
items.why: False. Beta cells in the pancreas sense glucose and release insulin with no order from the brain. Many cells run their own loops.

items.p: Sort each event: disturbance, or response?
items.why: A disturbance pushes the level away from the set point from outside the loop. A response is what the loop's effector does to bring it back.

items.p: A glucose sensor, a computer program and an insulin pump work together. Which loop job does each one do?
items.a: The sensor under her skin detects glucose. The computer program compares the reading with a target and decides. The pump is the effector and gives insulin. Her own liver, muscle and fat cells then take glucose in.
items.why: A strong answer matches sensor, control and effector to the three machine parts, and notices that her body's cells still do the final work.

items.p: James Watt's governor had two spinning balls. What did the balls sense?
items.why: The faster the engine turned, the further the balls swung out. Their height showed the speed, and a lever used it to move the steam valve.

items.p: Put these in order, for how a bacterium uses feedback to find sugar.
a: The bacterium senses the sugar level now
They compare it with the level a few seconds ago
If it is rising, they keep swimming straight
They reset their sensors to the new level
items.why: The comparison with a moment ago tells the bacterium whether things are getting better. Resetting the sensors lets them detect the next small change.

items.p: An AC whose compressor changes speed instead of switching on and off is called an ____ AC.
items.why: An inverter air conditioner runs its compressor fast when the error is large and slowly when it is small. That is how-much control.

items.p: Some scientists say the brain stores no set point for temperature. What, then, keeps the body near 37 degrees?
items.a: They say that sweating, shivering and skin blood flow are separate loops, each switching on at its own temperature. All of them respond to the same body temperature, and their combined action holds it near 37 degrees.
items.why: A strong answer says that the steady level comes from several loops acting together, and not from one stored number.

items.p: A pencil with forks hanging below it stays up with your eyes shut. What kind of steadiness is this?
opts: Steady by a fast feedback loop
Steady by its shape, with no loop
items.why: With the weight below the support, a lean swings back by itself. No sensing or correcting is needed.

items.p: True or false: positive feedback makes a change smaller.
items.why: False. Positive feedback makes a change bigger. The squeal of a microphone held near its loudspeaker is positive feedback.

items.p: Draw the loop for standing up. Show the neck arteries, the brainstem and the heart, with arrows for the messages.
items.a: A body outline with sensors marked in the neck arteries, an arrow from them up to the brainstem, an arrow from the brainstem down to the heart and to small arteries, and an arrow from the heart back to the pressure in the neck arteries.
items.why: A strong drawing closes the circle. The heart's faster beat raises the pressure, and the neck sensors detect that rise.

items.p: A thermostat acts until the room reaches 24 degrees, and then stops. Two views on what that means.

views.says: Acting towards a goal by negative feedback is what purpose is. A machine with feedback has a purpose in this sense.
The machine only behaves as if it had a purpose. Purpose needs someone who wants the goal.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with more? Give a reason from something you saw or did in this lesson.
items.a: Answers vary. A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason, such as the iron holding its temperature with no one watching, or the difference between a bacterium seeking sugar and a float valve.
items.why: This question is not settled. What matters is that the reason uses evidence, and that the answer says what 'purpose' is taken to mean.

items.p: Match each machine to the part that does its sensing.
items.why: The balls swing out with speed, the strip bends with heat, the float rises with water, and the skin sensor reads glucose. Each turns one kind of change into a movement or a signal.

items.p: Warm weather wears rock away faster, which removes carbon dioxide and cools the Earth. What is this?
items.why: The response acts against the warming, so it is negative feedback. It works over hundreds of thousands of years.

quiz.p: Which part of a feedback loop compares the level with what is needed?
quiz.why: The control centre receives the sensor's report, compares it with the level that is needed and sends an order. Choosing 'sensor' mixes up detecting with deciding.

quiz.p: Sweat glands carry out an order from the brain. Which job in the loop is that?
quiz.why: An effector acts and so changes the level. Sweat glands, muscles and the heart are effectors.

quiz.p: What makes a system a closed loop?
opts: News of its result changes its action
quiz.why: A closed loop measures its own result and adjusts. An open loop acts without checking.

quiz.p: Which of these is an open loop?
quiz.why: A mixer-grinder runs while the switch is held, whatever is in the jar. A fridge and a flush tank both check their own result.

quiz.p: Why is a metre stick easier to balance on your palm than a pencil?
quiz.why: A long stick takes longer to tip, so your eyes and hand have time for several corrections. Choosing 'heavier' is a common guess, but a heavy short stick is still hard.

quiz.p: A loop's sensor stops working. What happens to the level?
quiz.why: With no news of the change, nothing corrects it. In the Stick Test, the stick fell soon after the eyes were shut.

quiz.p: When you stand up, what first detects that blood pressure has dropped?
opts: Stretch sensors in the neck arteries
quiz.why: Baroreceptors in the walls of the neck arteries and the large artery from the heart detect the drop and signal the brainstem.

quiz.p: In a flush tank, which part is the sensor?
quiz.why: The float rides on the water, so its height shows the water level. The tap is the effector. The handle only starts the flush.

quiz.p: An iron's light goes on and off. What kind of control is this?
quiz.why: The heater is either fully on or fully off, and a switch moved by a bimetallic strip decides which.

quiz.p: Which of these senses glucose and releases insulin with no order from the brain?
opts: A beta cell in the pancreas
quiz.why: A beta cell is a sensor and a control in one cell. It shows that not every loop passes through the brain.

quiz.p: You timed a stick 5 times. Why find the mean and not use the best try?
opts: One try can be lucky or unlucky
quiz.why: A single try can be unusually good or bad. The mean of several tries is a fairer picture of what usually happens.

applications: A flush tank and the float valve in an overhead water tank shut off the water at a set level, so that tanks do not overflow.
Fridges, irons, geysers, ovens and air conditioners all hold a temperature with a thermostat.
A voltage stabiliser senses the mains voltage and corrects it, to protect a fridge or a television.
Closed-loop insulin pumps join a glucose sensor to a pump, for people with type 1 diabetes.
A pacemaker senses the heart's own beat and gives a small electric pulse only when a beat is missing.
An aircraft's autopilot senses height and direction many times a second and moves the wing flaps and the rudder to correct them.
Cruise control in a car senses the speed and gives more or less fuel to hold it, uphill and downhill.
Doctors and nurses check pulse, temperature and blood pressure because a level that has drifted shows which loop is struggling.

open_questions.q: Is there one set point for body temperature in the brain, or only many loops that add up to 37 degrees?
open_questions.why_open: Nobody has found a stored number. Models with separate loops fit many measurements, but how the loops stay in step is still argued over.

open_questions.q: What sets a person's blood pressure over years, and why do the neck sensors not correct high blood pressure?
open_questions.why_open: The baroreceptors slowly get used to a new pressure and stop reporting it as high. Whether the kidneys or the brain set the long-term level is still debated.

open_questions.q: How do giraffes keep blood reaching the brain when they raise their heads after drinking?
open_questions.why_open: The pressure in a drinking giraffe's head has been measured in very few animals. Several explanations exist and none is settled.

open_questions.q: Can a machine fully close the glucose loop for a person with diabetes, with no help at meal times?
open_questions.why_open: Insulin put under the skin acts more slowly than insulin from the pancreas. That delay makes a fully automatic loop hard to keep steady.

open_questions.q: Does life help to hold the Earth's temperature steady, or is the Earth's steadiness partly luck?
open_questions.why_open: Some loops are known, such as the wearing away of rock. Whether they would have saved life every time is impossible to test on one planet.

open_questions.q: How did the first feedback loop arise in the earliest cells?
open_questions.why_open: Every cell alive today already has thousands of loops. No simpler stage survives to be studied, so scientists can only build models.

maths.problem: In the Stick Test, Kavya's five tries with the long stick lasted 6, 9, 12, 8 and 10 seconds. What is the mean?
maths.explain: Add the five tries: 6 + 9 + 12 + 8 + 10 = 45. Divide by the number of tries: 45 ÷ 5 = 9. So the mean is 9 seconds.
maths.context: This is about the Stick Test. You balance a stick on your palm, and a helper times how long it stays up.
maths.why_maths: Balancing times jump about from try to try. The mean of five tries is a fairer number to compare sticks with.

chart.title: Made-up example: five tries with the long stick

maths.problem: In the Stand-Up Test, a helper counted 19 beats in 15 seconds lying down, and 25 beats in the first 15 seconds of standing. How many beats a minute is each? How big was the rise?
maths.answer: 76 beats a minute lying and 100 beats a minute standing. The rise was 24 beats a minute.
maths.explain: 15 seconds is a quarter of a minute, so multiply each count by 4. 19 × 4 = 76. 25 × 4 = 100. The rise is 100 − 76 = 24 beats a minute.
maths.context: This is about the Stand-Up Test. A helper counts your pulse at the wrist for 15 seconds, lying down and then just after you stand.
maths.why_maths: A pulse changes quickly after standing, so you can count for only 15 seconds. Multiplying by 4 turns that count into beats a minute.

maths.problem: In the Iron Light Test, at a low setting the light was on for 20 seconds and off for 100 seconds in each cycle. At a high setting it was on for 30 seconds and off for 60 seconds. For what fraction of the time was the heater on at each setting? How do the two compare?
maths.answer: One sixth of the time at the low setting, and one third at the high setting. The heater was on for twice as large a share of the time at the high setting.
maths.explain: Low setting: one cycle lasts 20 + 100 = 120 seconds, and 20 out of 120 is 20/120 = 1/6. High setting: one cycle lasts 30 + 60 = 90 seconds, and 30 out of 90 is 30/90 = 1/3. One third is twice one sixth.
maths.context: This is about the Iron Light Test. A grown-up runs an iron, and you time how long its indicator light stays on and off. These numbers are made up.
maths.why_maths: The 'on' times alone can mislead, because the cycles have different lengths. A fraction shows the share of the time the heater works.

maths.problem: Your eyes, brain and hand take about 0.2 seconds for one correction. A pencil tips too far in about 0.25 seconds. A metre stick tips too far in about 0.6 seconds. How many whole corrections fit in each time? What does that explain?
maths.answer: One correction for the pencil and three for the metre stick. It explains why the long stick is easier to balance.
maths.explain: Pencil: 0.25 ÷ 0.2 = 1.25, so only 1 whole correction fits. Metre stick: 0.6 ÷ 0.2 = 3, so 3 corrections fit. One correction is rarely enough to save a stick. Three give you a good chance.
maths.context: This is about the Stick Test, where a pencil fell much sooner than a long stick. The times here are rounded.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one time by the other shows how many times the loop can go round before it is too late. That turns 'too fast' into a number.

maths.problem: In the Bowl That Refills Itself, the water in the bottle stood 19 centimetres high on the first morning. It fell 3 centimetres each day. The hole is 1 centimetre above the base. On which day will the plate start to dry?
maths.explain: The bottle can give water until its level reaches the hole at 1 centimetre. That is 19 − 1 = 18 centimetres of water. At 3 centimetres a day, 18 ÷ 3 = 6 days. So the bottle keeps the plate full for 6 whole days, and the plate starts to dry on day 7.
maths.context: This is about the Bowl That Refills Itself. A bottle with a hole near its base keeps the water in a plate at one level. These numbers are made up.
maths.why_maths: A level that falls by the same amount each day makes a pattern. The pattern lets you predict when the loop will run out of water.

maths.problem: In Drift, Bang or Nudge, Meera's total gap was 14 in the Drift round and 19 in the Bang round. She played Drift three more times and scored 52, 38 and 47. What is her mean for the four Drift rounds? Was Drift really steadier than Bang?
maths.answer: The mean is 37.75. No. The first Drift round was a lucky one.
maths.explain: Add the four Drift totals: 14 + 52 + 38 + 47 = 151. Divide by 4: 151 ÷ 4 = 37.75. That is about twice her Bang total of 19. One round of 12 dice rolls can come out unusually low by chance. Several rounds show what usually happens.
maths.context: This is about the dice game Drift, Bang or Nudge. A die pushes a counter away from square 10, and you add up how far away it was each turn. A lower total means a steadier counter.
maths.why_maths: One odd result can point the wrong way. Repeating and finding the mean shows whether the result was a pattern or luck.

warmup.q: What are the three jobs in every feedback loop?
warmup.a: Sensing, deciding and acting. The parts are the sensor, the control centre and the effector.
News about the result of an action that comes back and changes the next action.

warmup.q: Is a fan with a regulator a closed loop or an open loop?
warmup.a: An open loop. It keeps its set speed and never checks the room.

warmup.q: Which is easier to balance on your palm, a pencil or a metre stick?
warmup.a: The metre stick. It tips more slowly, so your loop has time to correct it.

warmup.q: What happens to your pulse when you stand up after lying down?
warmup.a: It speeds up within seconds, to keep blood reaching your brain.

warmup.q: Where are the sensors that detect a drop in blood pressure?
warmup.a: In the walls of the neck arteries and of the large artery leaving the heart.

warmup.q: What bends inside an iron to switch the heater off?
warmup.a: A bimetallic strip, which is two metals joined together.

warmup.q: Name a loop in the body that works without the brain.
warmup.a: The glucose loop. Beta cells in the pancreas sense glucose and release insulin.

quiz: Every feedback loop needs something that senses a change.
Without a sensor, nothing knows that the level has moved.
A mixer-grinder checks whether the chutney is smooth and then stops.
A mixer-grinder is an open loop. It runs for as long as the switch is held.
A long stick is harder to balance on your palm than a pencil.
A long stick tips more slowly, so there is time to correct it.
Your pulse speeds up in the first seconds after you stand up.
Gravity pulls blood towards the legs, and the heart beats faster to keep the pressure up.
The sensors for blood pressure are in the leg muscles.
They are stretch sensors in the walls of the neck arteries and the large artery from the heart.
An iron's heater switches fully on and fully off.
A bimetallic strip opens and closes a switch. This is on-off control.
Negative feedback makes a change bigger.
Negative feedback acts against a change. Positive feedback makes a change bigger.
A single cell in the pancreas can sense glucose and respond.
A beta cell detects glucose and releases insulin with no order from the brain.
A street light with a light sensor is a closed loop.
The lamp does not change the daylight its sensor measures, so no news of its result comes back.
A loop with a long delay can make a level swing back and forth.
A late correction answers where the level was, not where it is now.
odd: A fridge, an iron and a flush tank are closed loops, but a mixer-grinder never checks its result.
A float, a baroreceptor and a bimetallic strip are sensors, but a heating coil is an effector.
Sweat glands, heart muscle and iris muscle are effectors, but the retina is a sensor.
The hypothalamus, the brainstem and a thermostat switch decide, but the kidney carries out the order.
The first three act against a change, but the squeal is positive feedback, which makes a change grow.

roots.context: We have learned that a level is held steady by a loop of sensing, deciding and acting. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In the Stick Test, the stick fell within a second or two when you shut your eyes. Your brain and your hand were as able as before. What had stopped was the news going round. In a feedback loop, each part acts only on what the part before it sends. So a steady level is made by the whole circle, and no single part is in charge of it.
deep_truth.habit: We look for the one part that is in charge: the brain in a body, the thermostat in a fridge. That picture has orders going one way, from a boss to workers. In a loop, the worker's result comes back and changes the next order, so the causes run in a circle.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Stick Test, removing only the news from the eyes made the stick fall. In Pour to the Line, the same hand poured well or badly depending on whether news of the level came back. In the Bowl That Refills Itself, the level held with no control part at all. In the pancreas, one beta cell is sensor and control together.

three.who_am_i: Hundreds of loops are holding you steady at this moment, and you started none of them on purpose. Part of what you call 'me' is this constant sensing and correcting.
three.what_is_life: Every living being, from a bacterium to a banyan tree, keeps their inside steady while the outside changes. Staying alive means sensing and correcting, all the time.
three.what_is_this_world: The same loop turns up in a cell, a body, an iron and perhaps the whole Earth. In each one, an effect comes back and becomes a cause.

roots.thread: Without a loop, a level goes wherever it is pushed. Join a sensor, a comparison and a response in a circle, and something new appears: a level that holds itself. That one pattern is found in a bacterium seeking sugar, in your pulse when you stand, in a flush tank and in a steam engine. The parts are different each time. The circle is the same. One way of working has become many kinds of steady things.

teachings.teaching: Returning is the movement of the Way.
teachings.link: Feedback means the result of an action returning to change the next action. A flush tank, a pulse and a boat held on a line across a river all stay steady because something returns.

teachings.teaching: The Buddha, just after his awakening, said: when this is, that is. When this arises, that arises.
teachings.link: In a loop nothing acts by itself. The heart speeds up because the brainstem signalled, the brainstem signalled because the sensors reported, and the sensors reported because of what the heart had done.

teachings.teaching: Find the illness, find its cause, find what will ease it, and then act in the way that fits.
teachings.link: Valluvar gives a healer three steps: notice, work out what is needed, and act. These are the three jobs of a loop, the sensor, the control and the effector, written down in Tamil long ago.

science.text: The same mathematics of feedback describes a bacterium resetting their sensors, the blood pressure loop of a human and the thermostat of a machine.
Rosenblueth, Wiener and Bigelow proposed in 1943 that purpose is behaviour steered by negative feedback from a goal. Whether that is all purpose is has been argued over ever since.

other_view.view: Causes never truly run in a circle. Each event is caused by an earlier one: the lean of the stick now causes the hand's move a fifth of a second later. The circle is only in our drawing. And some parts do matter more than others. Damage to the brainstem stops many loops at once, and damage to one sweat gland stops none.

practice.title: Feel a loop between your breath and your heart
practice.say: Sit comfortably. Find your pulse at your wrist with two fingers. Now breathe in slowly while I count to four. Breathe out slowly while I count to six. Keep going, and feel the beats. In many children the beats come a little closer together on the in-breath. They spread out a little on the out-breath. You may feel it, or you may not. Either way, your heart and your breathing are joined by loops in your brainstem. They are working now, and you did not start them.
practice.kid: Sit still. Find your pulse at your wrist. Breathe in slowly for four counts. Breathe out slowly for six counts. Feel the beats. Do they come closer together when you breathe in? You did not ask your heart to do that.

playtest: The experiments, activities, games and challenges in this lesson were reasoned through step by step as a family in a city flat would do them. They have not yet been tried at home, so please treat times and amounts as a starting point. The Stick Test (in the core path) needs a pencil, a 30 centimetre ruler and any straight stick about 1 metre long. A broom handle works. The palm must stay open, and the ceiling fan must be off. Pencil times are often under one second, and that is the expected result. With eyes shut, stand close and catch the stick. Pour to the Line is done with cool water over a tray. Some children stop by ear, and the step says what to do then. The Stand-Up Test needs a helper to count the pulse, because the first count must start within about 5 seconds of standing. A child who feels dizzy sits down at once. Pulse is felt at the wrist only, never at the neck. The Iron Light Test is done by a grown-up. Irons differ a great deal: at a low setting the light may stay off for several minutes, so the step allows timing one cycle. An iron without a light can be followed by the click of its switch. In the Bowl That Refills Itself, the cap must be airtight and the plate rim must be higher than the hole. Empty and scrub the plates after three days because of mosquitoes. Drift, Bang or Nudge was checked by running the three rules 2,000 times on a computer: the mean total gap was about 48 for Drift, 18 for Bang and 9 for Nudge, but a single round of 12 turns can come out in a different order. Loop Families was read through for a full game but not played with a real family. In the Short Stick Problem, the potato and forks stand on a fingertip only if the fork handles hang lower than the pencil point. Facts checked by web search while writing: Hering's 1923 work on the carotid sinus and his correction of Czermak's vagus explanation, the 1938 Nobel Prize to Heymans, the rise in pulse on standing in healthy children, the stick-balancing research on reaction delay and stick length, Watt's governor of 1788, Ktesibios's float regulator, Maxwell's 'On Governors' of 1868, Wiener's naming of cybernetics, Anand and Brobeck's 1951 paper, glucokinase as the beta cell's glucose sensor, the 2000 paper on integral feedback in E. coli, Romanovsky's 2007 paper, the 1943 and 1950 papers on purpose, the 1974 Gaia and 1981 rock-weathering papers, giraffe blood pressure, and the wording and numbering of Tao Te Ching 40, Udana 1.1 and Thirukkural 948. The three video addresses were confirmed by title and channel but the videos were not watched. Not confirmed by a search, and written from general knowledge: the exact decade of Czermak's observation (given as the 1860s), the times a pencil and a metre stick take to tip (worked out from school physics and rounded), and that astronauts often feel faint on first standing after long flights.
